sections.title: Factor Trinomials using Trial and Error
sections.paragraph: What happens when the leading coefficient is not 1 and there is no GCF? There are several methods that can be used to factor these trinomials. First we will use the Trial and Error method.

sections.title: Factor Trinomials using the “ac” Method
sections.paragraph: Another way to factor trinomials of the form $a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ is the “ac” method. (The “ac” method is sometimes called the grouping method.) The “ac” method is actually an extension of the methods you used in the last section to factor trinomials with leading coefficient one. This method is very structured (that is step-by-step), and it always works!

chapters.title: Factor Special Products
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Factor perfect square trinomials
* Factor differences of squares
* Factor sums and differences of cubes
* Choose method to factor a polynomial completely

sections.title: Factor Perfect Square Trinomials
sections.paragraph: Some trinomials are perfect squares. They result from multiplying a binomial times itself. You can square a binomial by using FOIL, but using the Binomial Squares pattern you saw in a previous chapter saves you a step. Let’s review the Binomial Squares pattern by squaring a binomial using FOIL.

sections.title: Factor Differences of Squares
sections.paragraph: The other special product you saw in the previous chapter was the Product of Conjugates pattern. You used this to multiply two binomials that were conjugates. Here’s an example:

sections.title: Factor Sums and Differences of Cubes
sections.paragraph: There is another special pattern for factoring, one that we did not use when we multiplied polynomials. This is the pattern for the sum and difference of cubes. We will write these formulas first and then check them by multiplication.

chapters.title: General Strategy for Factoring Polynomials
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Recognize and use the appropriate method to factor a polynomial completely

sections.title: Recognize and Use the Appropriate Method to Factor a Polynomial Completely
sections.paragraph: You have now become acquainted with all the methods of factoring that you will need in this course. (In your next algebra course, more methods will be added to your repertoire.) The figure below summarizes all the factoring methods we have covered. [link] outlines a strategy you should use when factoring polynomials.

chapters.title: Quadratic Equations
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve quadratic equations by using the Zero Product Property
* Solve quadratic equations factoring
* Solve applications modeled by quadratic equations

sections.title: Solve Quadratic Equations Using the Zero Product Property
sections.paragraph: We will first solve some quadratic equations by using the Zero Product Property. The Zero Product Property says that if the product of two quantities is zero, it must be that at least one of the quantities is zero. The only way to get a product equal to zero is to multiply by zero itself.

sections.title: Solve Quadratic Equations by Factoring
sections.paragraph: Each of the equations we have solved in this section so far had one side in factored form. In order to use the Zero Product Property, the quadratic equation must be factored, with zero on one side. So we must be sure to start with the quadratic equation in standard form, $a{x}^{2}+bx+c=0$. Then we can factor the expression on the left.

sections.title: Solve Applications Modeled by Quadratic Equations
sections.paragraph: The problem solving strategy we used earlier for applications that translate to linear equations will work just as well for applications that translate to quadratic equations. We will copy the problem solving strategy here so we can use it for reference.

chapters.title: Simplify Rational Expressions
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Determine the values for which a rational expression is undefined
* Evaluate rational expressions
* Simplify rational expressions
* Simplify rational expressions with opposite factors

sections.title: Determine the Values for Which a Rational Expression is Undefined
sections.paragraph: When we work with a numerical fraction, it is easy to avoid dividing by zero, because we can see the number in the denominator. In order to avoid dividing by zero in a rational expression, we must not allow values of the variable that will make the denominator be zero.

sections.title: Evaluate Rational Expressions
sections.paragraph: To evaluate a rational expression, we substitute values of the variables into the expression and simplify, just as we have for many other expressions in this book.

sections.title: Simplify Rational Expressions
sections.paragraph: Just like a fraction is considered simplified if there are no common factors, other than 1, in its numerator and denominator, a rational expression is *simplified* if it has no common factors, other than 1, in its numerator and denominator.

sections.title: Simplify Rational Expressions with Opposite Factors
sections.paragraph: Now we will see how to simplify a rational expression whose numerator and denominator have opposite factors. Let’s start with a numerical fraction, say $\frac{7}{-7}$. We know this fraction simplifies to $-1$. We also recognize that the numerator and denominator are opposites.

chapters.title: Multiply and Divide Rational Expressions
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Multiply rational expressions
* Divide rational expressions

sections.title: Multiply Rational Expressions
sections.paragraph: To multiply rational expressions, we do just what we did with numerical fractions. We multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators. Then, if there are any common factors, we remove them to simplify the result.

sections.title: Divide Rational Expressions
sections.paragraph: To divide rational expressions we multiply the first fraction by the reciprocal of the second, just like we did for numerical fractions.

chapters.title: Add and Subtract Rational Expressions with a Common Denominator
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Add rational expressions with a common denominator
* Subtract rational expressions with a common denominator
* Add and subtract rational expressions whose denominators are opposites

sections.title: Add Rational Expressions with a Common Denominator
sections.paragraph: What is the first step you take when you add numerical fractions? You check if they have a common denominator. If they do, you add the numerators and place the sum over the common denominator. If they do not have a common denominator, you find one before you add.

sections.title: Subtract Rational Expressions with a Common Denominator
sections.paragraph: To subtract rational expressions, they must also have a common denominator. When the denominators are the same, you subtract the numerators and place the difference over the common denominator.

sections.title: Add and Subtract Rational Expressions whose Denominators are Opposites
sections.paragraph: When the denominators of two rational expressions are opposites, it is easy to get a common denominator. We just have to multiply one of the fractions by $\frac{-1}{-1}$.

chapters.title: Add and Subtract Rational Expressions with Unlike Denominators
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Find the least common denominator of rational expressions
* Find equivalent rational expressions
* Add rational expressions with different denominators
* Subtract rational expressions with different denominators

sections.title: Find the Least Common Denominator of Rational Expressions
sections.paragraph: When we add or subtract rational expressions with unlike denominators we will need to get common denominators. If we review the procedure we used with numerical fractions, we will know what to do with rational expressions.

sections.title: Find Equivalent Rational Expressions
sections.paragraph: When we add numerical fractions, once we find the LCD, we rewrite each fraction as an equivalent fraction with the LCD.

sections.title: Add Rational Expressions with Different Denominators
sections.paragraph: Now we have all the steps we need to add rational expressions with different denominators. As we have done previously, we will do one example of adding numerical fractions first.

sections.title: Subtract Rational Expressions with Different Denominators
sections.paragraph: The process we use to subtract rational expressions with different denominators is the same as for addition. We just have to be very careful of the signs when subtracting the numerators.

chapters.title: Simplify Complex Rational Expressions
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Simplify a complex rational expression by writing it as division
* Simplify a complex rational expression by using the LCD

sections.title: Simplify a Complex Rational Expression by Writing it as Division
sections.paragraph: We have already seen this complex rational expression earlier in this chapter.

sections.title: Simplify a Complex Rational Expression by Using the LCD
sections.paragraph: We “cleared” the fractions by multiplying by the LCD when we solved equations with fractions. We can use that strategy here to simplify complex rational expressions. We will multiply the numerator and denominator by LCD of all the rational expressions.

chapters.title: Solve Rational Equations
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve rational equations
* Solve a rational equation for a specific variable

sections.title: Solve Rational Equations
sections.paragraph: We have already solved linear equations that contained fractions. We found the LCD of all the fractions in the equation and then multiplied both sides of the equation by the LCD to “clear” the fractions.

sections.title: Solve a Rational Equation for a Specific Variable
sections.paragraph: When we solved linear equations, we learned how to solve a formula for a specific variable. Many formulas used in business, science, economics, and other fields use rational equations to model the relation between two or more variables. We will now see how to solve a rational equation for a specific variable.

chapters.title: Solve Proportion and Similar Figure Applications
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve proportions
* Solve similar figure applications

sections.title: Solve Proportions
sections.paragraph: When two rational expressions are equal, the equation relating them is called a *proportion*.

sections.title: Solve Similar Figure Applications
sections.paragraph: When you shrink or enlarge a photo on a phone or tablet, figure out a distance on a map, or use a pattern to build a bookcase or sew a dress, you are working with similar figures. If two figures have exactly the same shape, but different sizes, they are said to be *similar.* One is a scale model of the other. All their corresponding angles have the same measures and their corresponding sides are in the same ratio.

chapters.title: Solve Uniform Motion and Work Applications
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve uniform motion applications
* Solve work applications

sections.title: Solve Uniform Motion Applications
sections.paragraph: We have solved uniform motion problems using the formula $D=rt$ in previous chapters. We used a table like the one below to organize the information and lead us to the equation.

sections.title: Solve Work Applications
sections.paragraph: Suppose Pete can paint a room in 10 hours. If he works at a steady pace, in 1 hour he would paint $\frac{1}{10}$ of the room. If Alicia would take 8 hours to paint the same room, then in 1 hour she would paint $\frac{1}{8}$ of the room. How long would it take Pete and Alicia to paint the room if they worked together (and didn’t interfere with each other’s progress)?

chapters.title: Use Direct and Inverse Variation
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve direct variation problems
* Solve inverse variation problems

sections.title: Solve Direct Variation Problems
sections.paragraph: Lindsay gets paid \$15 per hour at her job. If we let *s* be her salary and *h* be the number of hours she has worked, we could model this situation with the equation

sections.title: Solve Inverse Variation Problems
sections.paragraph: Many applications involve two variable that *vary inversely*. As one variable increases, the other decreases. The equation that relates them is $y=\frac{k}{x}$.

chapters.title: Simplify and Use Square Roots
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Simplify expressions with square roots
* Estimate square roots
* Approximate square roots
* Simplify variable expressions with square roots

sections.title: Simplify Expressions with Square Roots
sections.paragraph: Remember that when a number $n$ is multiplied by itself, we write ${n}^{2}$ and read it “n squared.” For example, ${15}^{2}$ reads as “15 squared,” and 225 is called the square of 15, since ${15}^{2}=225$.

sections.title: Estimate Square Roots
sections.paragraph: So far we have only considered square roots of perfect square numbers. The square roots of other numbers are not whole numbers. Look at [link] below.

sections.title: Approximate Square Roots
sections.paragraph: There are mathematical methods to approximate square roots, but nowadays most people use a calculator to find them. Find the $\sqrt{x}$ key on your calculator. You will use this key to approximate square roots.

sections.title: Simplify Variable Expressions with Square Roots
sections.paragraph: What if we have to find a square root of an expression with a variable? Consider $\sqrt{9{x}^{2}}$. Can you think of an expression whose square is $9{x}^{2}$?

chapters.title: Simplify Square Roots
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Use the Product Property to simplify square roots
* Use the Quotient Property to simplify square roots

sections.title: Use the Product Property to Simplify Square Roots
sections.paragraph: The properties we will use to simplify expressions with square roots are similar to the properties of exponents. We know that ${\left(ab\right)}^{m}={a}^{m}{b}^{m}$. The corresponding property of square roots says that $\sqrt{ab}=\sqrt{a}·\sqrt{b}$.

sections.title: Use the Quotient Property to Simplify Square Roots
sections.paragraph: Whenever you have to simplify a square root, the first step you should take is to determine whether the radicand is a perfect square. A *perfect square fraction* is a fraction in which both the numerator and the denominator are perfect squares.

chapters.title: Add and Subtract Square Roots
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Add and subtract like square roots
* Add and subtract square roots that need simplification

sections.title: Add and Subtract Like Square Roots
sections.paragraph: Think about adding like terms with variables as you do the next few examples. When you have like radicands, you just add or subtract the coefficients. When the radicands are not like, you cannot combine the terms.

sections.title: Add and Subtract Square Roots that Need Simplification
sections.paragraph: Remember that we always simplify square roots by removing the largest perfect-square factor. Sometimes when we have to add or subtract square roots that do not appear to have like radicals, we find like radicals after simplifying the square roots.

chapters.title: Multiply Square Roots
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Multiply square roots
* Use polynomial multiplication to multiply square roots

sections.title: Multiply Square Roots
sections.paragraph: We have used the Product Property of Square Roots to simplify square roots by removing the perfect square factors. The Product Property of Square Roots says

sections.title: Use Polynomial Multiplication to Multiply Square Roots
sections.paragraph: In the next few examples, we will use the Distributive Property to multiply expressions with square roots.

chapters.title: Divide Square Roots
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Divide square roots
* Rationalize a one-term denominator
* Rationalize a two-term denominator

sections.title: Divide Square Roots
sections.paragraph: We know that we simplify fractions by removing factors common to the numerator and the denominator. When we have a fraction with a square root in the numerator, we first simplify the square root. Then we can look for common factors.

sections.title: Rationalize a One Term Denominator
sections.paragraph: Before the calculator became a tool of everyday life, tables of square roots were used to find approximate values of square roots. [link] shows a portion of a table of squares and square roots. Square roots are approximated to five decimal places in this table.

sections.title: Rationalize a Two-Term Denominator
sections.paragraph: When the denominator of a fraction is a sum or difference with square roots, we use the Product of Conjugates pattern to rationalize the denominator.

chapters.title: Solve Equations with Square Roots
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve radical equations
* Use square roots in applications

sections.title: Solve Radical Equations
sections.paragraph: In this section we will solve equations that have the variable in the radicand of a square root. Equations of this type are called radical equations.

sections.title: Use Square Roots in Applications
sections.paragraph: As you progress through your college courses, you’ll encounter formulas that include square roots in many disciplines. We have already used formulas to solve geometry applications.

chapters.title: Higher Roots
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Simplify expressions with higher roots
* Use the Product Property to simplify expressions with higher roots
* Use the Quotient Property to simplify expressions with higher roots
* Add and subtract higher roots

sections.title: Simplify Expressions with Higher Roots
sections.paragraph: Up to now, in this chapter we have worked with squares and square roots. We will now extend our work to include higher powers and higher roots.

sections.title: Use the Product Property to Simplify Expressions with Higher Roots
sections.paragraph: We will simplify expressions with higher roots in much the same way as we simplified expressions with square roots. An *n*th root is considered simplified if it has no factors of ${m}^{n}$.

sections.title: Use the Quotient Property to Simplify Expressions with Higher Roots
sections.paragraph: We can simplify higher roots with quotients in the same way we simplified square roots. First we simplify any fractions inside the radical.

sections.title: Add and Subtract Higher Roots
sections.paragraph: We can add and subtract higher roots like we added and subtracted square roots. First we provide a formal definition of like radicals.

chapters.title: Rational Exponents
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Simplify expressions with ${a}^{\frac{1}{n}}$
* Simplify expressions with ${a}^{\frac{m}{n}}$
* Use the Laws of Exponents to simply expressions with rational exponents

sections.title: Simplify Expressions with ${a}^{\frac{1}{n}}$
sections.paragraph: Rational exponents are another way of writing expressions with radicals. When we use rational exponents, we can apply the properties of exponents to simplify expressions.

sections.title: Simplify Expressions with ${a}^{\frac{m}{n}}$
sections.paragraph: Let’s work with the Power Property for Exponents some more.

sections.title: Use the Laws of Exponents to Simplify Expressions with Rational Exponents
sections.paragraph: The same laws of exponents that we already used apply to rational exponents, too. We will list the Exponent Properties here to have them for reference as we simplify expressions.

chapters.title: Solve Quadratic Equations Using the Square Root Property
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve quadratic equations of the form $a{x}^{2}=k$ using the Square Root Property
* Solve quadratic equations of the form $a{\left(x-h\right)}^{2}=k$ using the Square Root Property

sections.title: Solve Quadratic Equations of the Form *ax*2 = *k* Using the Square Root Property
sections.paragraph: We have already solved some quadratic equations by factoring. Let’s review how we used factoring to solve the quadratic equation ${x}^{2}=9$.

sections.title: Solve Quadratic Equations of the Form *a*(*x* − *h*)2 = *k* Using the Square Root Property
sections.paragraph: We can use the Square Root Property to solve an equation like ${\left(x-3\right)}^{2}=16$, too. We will treat the whole binomial, $\left(x-3\right)$, as the quadratic term.

chapters.title: Solve Quadratic Equations by Completing the Square
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Complete the square of a binomial expression
* Solve quadratic equations of the form ${x}^{2}+bx+c=0$ by completing the square
* Solve quadratic equations of the form $a{x}^{2}+bx+c=0$ by completing the square

sections.title: Complete The Square of a Binomial Expression
sections.paragraph: In the last section, we were able to use the Square Root Property to solve the equation ${\left(y-7\right)}^{2}=12$ because the left side was a perfect square.

sections.title: Solve Quadratic Equations of the Form *x*2 + *bx* + *c* = 0 by completing the square
sections.paragraph: In solving equations, we must always do the same thing to both sides of the equation. This is true, of course, when we solve a quadratic equation by completing the square, too. When we add a term to one side of the equation to make a perfect square trinomial, we must also add the same term to the other side of the equation.

sections.title: Solve Quadratic Equations of the form *ax*2 + *bx* + *c* = 0 by completing the square
sections.paragraph: The process of completing the square works best when the leading coefficient is one, so the left side of the equation is of the form ${x}^{2}+bx+c$. If the ${x}^{2}$ term has a coefficient, we take some preliminary steps to make the coefficient equal to one.

chapters.title: Solve Quadratic Equations Using the Quadratic Formula
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve quadratic equations using the quadratic formula
* Use the discriminant to predict the number of solutions of a quadratic equation
* Identify the most appropriate method to use to solve a quadratic equation

sections.title: Use the Discriminant to Predict the Number of Solutions of a Quadratic Equation
sections.paragraph: When we solved the quadratic equations in the previous examples, sometimes we got two solutions, sometimes one solution, sometimes no real solutions. Is there a way to predict the number of solutions to a quadratic equation without actually solving the equation?

sections.title: Identify the Most Appropriate Method to Use to Solve a Quadratic Equation
sections.paragraph: We have used four methods to solve quadratic equations:

chapters.title: Solve Applications Modeled by Quadratic Equations
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve applications modeled by Quadratic Equations

sections.title: Solve Applications of the Quadratic Formula
sections.paragraph: We solved some applications that are modeled by quadratic equations earlier, when the only method we had to solve them was factoring. Now that we have more methods to solve quadratic equations, we will take another look at applications. To get us started, we will copy our usual Problem Solving Strategy here so we can follow the steps.

chapters.title: Graphing Quadratic Equations in Two Variables
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Recognize the graph of a quadratic equation in two variables
* Find the axis of symmetry and vertex of a parabola
* Find the intercepts of a parabola
* Graph quadratic equations in two variables
* Solve maximum and minimum applications

sections.title: Recognize the Graph of a Quadratic Equation in Two Variables
sections.paragraph: We have graphed equations of the form $Ax+By=C$. We called equations like this linear equations because their graphs are straight lines.

sections.title: Find the Axis of Symmetry and Vertex of a Parabola
sections.paragraph: Look again at [link]. Do you see that we could fold each parabola in half and that one side would lie on top of the other? The ‘fold line’ is a line of symmetry. We call it the axis of symmetry of the parabola.

sections.title: Find the Intercepts of a Parabola
sections.paragraph: When we graphed linear equations, we often used the *x*- and *y*-intercepts to help us graph the lines. Finding the coordinates of the intercepts will help us to graph parabolas, too.

sections.title: Graph Quadratic Equations in Two Variables
sections.paragraph: Now, we have all the pieces we need in order to graph a quadratic equation in two variables. We just need to put them together. In the next example, we will see how to do this.

sections.title: Solve Maximum and Minimum Applications
sections.paragraph: Knowing that the vertex of a parabola is the lowest or highest point of the parabola gives us an easy way to determine the minimum or maximum value of a quadratic equation. The *y*-coordinate of the vertex is the minimum *y*-value of a parabola that opens upward. It is the maximum *y*-value of a parabola that opens downward. See [link].

sections.title: About OpenStax
sections.paragraph: OpenStax is a nonprofit based at Rice University, and it’s our mission to improve student access to education. Our first openly licensed college textbook was published in 2012, and our library has since scaled to over 35 books for college and AP courses used by hundreds of thousands of students. Our adaptive learning technology, designed to improve learning outcomes through personalized educational paths, is being piloted in college courses throughout the country. Through our partnerships with philanthropic foundations and our alliance with other educational resource organizations, OpenStax is breaking down the most common barriers to learning and empowering students and instructors to succeed.

sections.title: About *Intermediate Algebra 2e*
sections.paragraph: *Intermediate Algebra 2e* is designed to meet the scope and sequence requirements of a one-semester Intermediate Algebra course. The book’s organization makes it easy to adapt to a variety of course syllabi. The text expands on the fundamental concepts of algebra while addressing the needs of students with diverse backgrounds and learning styles. Each topic builds upon previously developed material to demonstrate the cohesiveness and structure of mathematics.

chapters.title: Use the Language of Algebra
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Find factors, prime factorizations, and least common multiples
* Use variables and algebraic symbols
* Simplify expressions using the order of operations
* Evaluate an expression
* Identify and combine like terms
* Translate an English phrase to an algebraic expression

sections.title: Find Factors, Prime Factorizations, and Least Common Multiples
sections.paragraph: The numbers 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 are called multiples of 2. A multiple of 2 can be written as the product of 2 and a counting number.

sections.title: Use Variables and Algebraic Symbols
sections.paragraph: In algebra, we use a letter of the alphabet to represent a number whose value may change. We call this a variable and letters commonly used for variables are $x,y,a,b,c.$

sections.title: Simplify Expressions Using the Order of Operations
sections.paragraph: To simplify an expression means to do all the math possible. For example, to simplify $4·2+1$ we would first multiply $4·2$ to get 8 and then add the 1 to get 9. A good habit to develop is to work down the page, writing each step of the process below the previous step. The example just described would look like this:

sections.title: Evaluate an Expression
sections.paragraph: In the last few examples, we simplified expressions using the order of operations. Now we’ll evaluate some expressions—again following the order of operations. To evaluate an expression means to find the value of the expression when the variable is replaced by a given number.

sections.title: Identify and Combine Like Terms
sections.paragraph: Algebraic expressions are made up of terms. A term is a constant, or the product of a constant and one or more variables.

sections.title: Translate an English Phrase to an Algebraic Expression
sections.paragraph: We listed many operation symbols that are used in algebra. Now, we will use them to translate English phrases into algebraic expressions. The symbols and variables we’ve talked about will help us do that. [link] summarizes them.

chapters.title: Integers
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Simplify expressions with absolute value
* Add and subtract integers
* Multiply and divide integers
* Simplify expressions with integers
* Evaluate variable expressions with integers
* Translate phrases to expressions with integers
* Use integers in applications

sections.title: Simplify Expressions with Absolute Value
sections.paragraph: A negative number is a number less than 0. The negative numbers are to the left of zero on the number line. See [link].

sections.title: Add and Subtract Integers
sections.paragraph: So far, we have only used the counting numbers and the whole numbers.

sections.title: Multiply and Divide Integers
sections.paragraph: Since multiplication is mathematical shorthand for repeated addition, our model can easily be applied to show multiplication of integers. Let’s look at this concrete model to see what patterns we notice. We will use the same examples that we used for addition and subtraction. Here, we are using the model just to help us discover the pattern.

sections.title: Simplify Expressions with Integers
sections.paragraph: What happens when there are more than two numbers in an expression? The order of operations still applies when negatives are included. Remember Please Excuse My Dear Aunt Sally?

sections.title: Evaluate Variable Expressions with Integers
sections.paragraph: Remember that to evaluate an expression means to substitute a number for the variable in the expression. Now we can use negative numbers as well as positive numbers.

sections.title: Translate Phrases to Expressions with Integers
sections.paragraph: Our earlier work translating English to algebra also applies to phrases that include both positive and negative numbers.

sections.title: Use Integers in Applications
sections.paragraph: We’ll outline a plan to solve applications. It’s hard to find something if we don’t know what we’re looking for or what to call it! So when we solve an application, we first need to determine what the problem is asking us to find. Then we’ll write a phrase that gives the information to find it. We’ll translate the phrase into an expression and then simplify the expression to get the answer. Finally, we summarize the answer in a sentence to make sure it makes sense.

chapters.title: Fractions
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Simplify fractions
* Multiply and divide fractions
* Add and subtract fractions
* Use the order of operations to simplify fractions
* Evaluate variable expressions with fractions

sections.title: Simplify Fractions
sections.paragraph: A fraction is a way to represent parts of a whole. The fraction $\frac{2}{3}$ represents two of three equal parts. See [link]. In the fraction $\frac{2}{3},$ the 2 is called the numerator and the 3 is called the denominator. The line is called the fraction bar.

sections.title: Multiply and Divide Fractions
sections.paragraph: Many people find multiplying and dividing fractions easier than adding and subtracting fractions.

sections.title: Add and Subtract Fractions
sections.paragraph: When we multiplied fractions, we just multiplied the numerators and multiplied the denominators right straight across. To add or subtract fractions, they must have a common denominator.

sections.title: Use the Order of Operations to Simplify Fractions
sections.paragraph: The fraction bar in a fraction acts as grouping symbol. The order of operations then tells us to simplify the numerator and then the denominator. Then we divide.

sections.title: Evaluate Variable Expressions with Fractions
sections.paragraph: We have evaluated expressions before, but now we can evaluate expressions with fractions. Remember, to evaluate an expression, we substitute the value of the variable into the expression and then simplify.

chapters.title: Decimals
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Round decimals
* Add and subtract decimals
* Multiply and divide decimals
* Convert decimals, fractions, and percents
* Simplify expressions with square roots
* Identify integers, rational numbers, irrational numbers, and real numbers
* Locate fractions and decimals on the number line

sections.title: Round Decimals
sections.paragraph: Decimals are another way of writing fractions whose denominators are powers of ten.

sections.title: Add and Subtract Decimals
sections.paragraph: To add or subtract decimals, we line up the decimal points. By lining up the decimal points this way, we can add or subtract the corresponding place values. We then add or subtract the numbers as if they were whole numbers and then place the decimal point in the sum.

sections.title: Multiply and Divide Decimals
sections.paragraph: When we multiply signed decimals, first we determine the sign of the product and then multiply as if the numbers were both positive. We multiply the numbers temporarily ignoring the decimal point and then count the number of decimal points in the factors and that sum tells us the number of decimal places in the product. Finally, we write the product with the appropriate sign.

sections.title: Convert Decimals, Fractions, and Percents
sections.paragraph: In our work, it is often necessary to change the form of a number. We may have to change fractions to decimals or decimals to percent.

sections.title: Simplify Expressions with Square Roots
sections.paragraph: Remember that when a number $n$ is multiplied by itself, we write ${n}^{2}$ and read it “$n$ squared.” The result is called the square of a number *n*. For example, ${8}^{2}$ is read “8 squared” and 64 is called the *square* of 8. Similarly, 121 is the square of 11 because ${11}^{2}$ is 121. It will be helpful to learn to recognize the perfect square numbers.

sections.title: Identify Integers, Rational Numbers, Irrational Numbers, and Real Numbers
sections.paragraph: We have already described numbers as *counting number**s*, *whole number**s*, and *integers*. What is the difference between these types of numbers? Difference could be confused with subtraction. How about asking how we distinguish between these types of numbers?

sections.title: Locate Fractions and Decimals on the Number Line
sections.paragraph: We now want to include fractions and decimals on the number line. Let’s start with fractions and locate $\frac{1}{5},-\frac{4}{5},3,\frac{7}{4},-\frac{9}{2},-5$ and $\frac{8}{3}$ on the number line.

chapters.title: Properties of Real Numbers
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Use the commutative and associative properties
* Use the properties of identity, inverse, and zero
* Simplify expressions using the Distributive Property

sections.title: Use the Commutative and Associative Properties
sections.paragraph: The order we add two numbers doesn’t affect the result. If we add $8+9$ or $9+8,$ the results are the same—they both equal 17. So, $8+9=9+8.$ The order in which we add does not matter!

sections.title: Use the Properties of Identity, Inverse, and Zero
sections.paragraph: What happens when we add 0 to any number? Adding 0 doesn’t change the value. For this reason, we call 0 the additive identity. The Identity Property of Addition that states that for any real number $a,a+0=a$ and $0+a=a.$

sections.title: Simplify Expressions Using the Distributive Property
sections.paragraph: Suppose that three friends are going to the movies. They each need \$9.25—that’s 9 dollars and 1 quarter—to pay for their tickets. How much money do they need all together?

chapters.title: Use a General Strategy to Solve Linear Equations
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve linear equations using a general strategy
* Classify equations
* Solve equations with fraction or decimal coefficients

sections.title: Solve Linear Equations Using a General Strategy
sections.paragraph: Solving an equation is like discovering the answer to a puzzle. The purpose in solving an equation is to find the value or values of the variable that makes it a true statement. Any value of the variable that makes the equation true is called a solution to the equation. It is the answer to the puzzle!

sections.title: Classify Equations
sections.paragraph: Whether or not an equation is true depends on the value of the variable. The equation $7x+8=-13$ is true when we replace the variable, *x*, with the value $-3,$ but not true when we replace *x* with any other value. An equation like this is called a conditional equation. All the equations we have solved so far are conditional equations.

sections.title: Solve Equations with Fraction or Decimal Coefficients
sections.paragraph: We could use the General Strategy to solve the next example. This method would work fine, but many students do not feel very confident when they see all those fractions. So, we are going to show an alternate method to solve equations with fractions. This alternate method eliminates the fractions.

chapters.title: Use a Problem Solving Strategy
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Use a problem solving strategy for word problems
* Solve number word problems
* Solve percent applications
* Solve simple interest applications

sections.title: Use a Problem Solving Strategy for Word Problems
sections.paragraph: Now that we can solve equations, we are ready to apply our new skills to word problems. We will develop a strategy we can use to solve any word problem successfully.

sections.title: Solve Number Word Problems
sections.paragraph: We will now apply the problem solving strategy to “number word problems.” Number word problems give some clues about one or more numbers and we use these clues to write an equation. Number word problems provide good practice for using the Problem Solving Strategy.

sections.title: Solve Percent Applications
sections.paragraph: There are several methods to solve percent equations. In algebra, it is easiest if we just translate English sentences into algebraic equations and then solve the equations. Be sure to change the given percent to a decimal before you use it in the equation.

sections.title: Solve Simple Interest Applications
sections.paragraph: Interest is a part of our daily lives. From the interest earned on our savings to the interest we pay on a car loan or credit card debt, we all have some experience with interest in our lives.

chapters.title: Solve a Formula for a Specific Variable
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve a formula for a specific variable
* Use formulas to solve geometry applications

sections.title: Solve a Formula for a Specific Variable
sections.paragraph: We have all probably worked with some geometric formulas in our study of mathematics. Formulas are used in so many fields, it is important to recognize formulas and be able to manipulate them easily.

sections.title: Use Formulas to Solve Geometry Applications
sections.paragraph: In this objective we will use some common geometry formulas. We will adapt our problem solving strategy so that we can solve geometry applications. The geometry formula will name the variables and give us the equation to solve.

chapters.title: Solve Mixture and Uniform Motion Applications
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve coin word problems
* Solve ticket and stamp word problems
* Solve mixture word problems
* Solve uniform motion applications

sections.title: Solve Coin Word Problems
sections.paragraph: Using algebra to find the number of nickels and pennies in a piggy bank may seem silly. You may wonder why we just don’t open the bank and count them. But this type of problem introduces us to some techniques that will be useful as we move forward in our study of mathematics.

sections.title: Solve Ticket and Stamp Word Problems
sections.paragraph: Problems involving tickets or stamps are very much like coin problems. Each type of ticket and stamp has a value, just like each type of coin does. So to solve these problems, we will follow the same steps we used to solve coin problems.

sections.title: Solve Mixture Word Problems
sections.paragraph: Now we’ll solve some more general applications of the mixture model. In mixture problems, we are often mixing two quantities, such as raisins and nuts, to create a mixture, such as trail mix. In our tables we will have a row for each item to be mixed as well as one for the final mixture.

sections.title: Solve Uniform Motion Applications
sections.paragraph: When you are driving down the interstate using your cruise control, the speed of your car stays the same—it is uniform. We call a problem in which the speed of an object is constant a uniform motion application. We will use the distance, rate, and time formula, $D=rt,$ to compare two scenarios, such as two vehicles travelling at different rates or in opposite directions.

chapters.title: Solve Linear Inequalities
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Graph inequalities on the number line
* Solve linear inequalities
* Translate words to an inequality and solve
* Solve applications with linear inequalities

sections.title: Graph Inequalities on the Number Line
sections.paragraph: What number would make the inequality $x>3$ true? Are you thinking, “*x* could be four”? That’s correct, but *x* could be 6, too, or 37, or even 3.001. Any number greater than three is a solution to the inequality $x>3.$

sections.title: Solve Linear Inequalities
sections.paragraph: A linear inequality is much like a linear equation—but the equal sign is replaced with an inequality sign. A **linear inequality** is an inequality in one variable that can be written in one of the forms, $ax+b$ax+b\le c,$$ax+b>c,$ or $ax+b\ge c.$

sections.title: Translate to an Inequality and Solve
sections.paragraph: To translate English sentences into inequalities, we need to recognize the phrases that indicate the inequality. Some words are easy, like “more than” and “less than.” But others are not as obvious. [link] shows some common phrases that indicate inequalities.

sections.title: Solve Applications with Linear Inequalities
sections.paragraph: Many real-life situations require us to solve inequalities. The method we will use to solve applications with linear inequalities is very much like the one we used when we solved applications with equations.

chapters.title: Solve Compound Inequalities
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve compound inequalities with “and”
* Solve compound inequalities with “or”
* Solve applications with compound inequalities

sections.title: Solve Compound Inequalities with “and”
sections.paragraph: Now that we know how to solve linear inequalities, the next step is to look at compound inequalities. A compound inequality is made up of two inequalities connected by the word “and” or the word “or.” For example, the following are compound inequalities.

sections.title: Solve Compound Inequalities with “or”
sections.paragraph: To solve a compound inequality with “or”, we start out just as we did with the compound inequalities with “and”—we solve the two inequalities. Then we find all the numbers that make *either* inequality true.

sections.title: Solve Applications with Compound Inequalities
sections.paragraph: Situations in the real world also involve compound inequalities. We will use the same problem solving strategy that we used to solve linear equation and inequality applications.

chapters.title: Solve Absolute Value Inequalities
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve absolute value equations
* Solve absolute value inequalities with “less than”
* Solve absolute value inequalities with “greater than”
* Solve applications with absolute value

sections.title: Solve Absolute Value Equations
sections.paragraph: As we prepare to solve absolute value equations, we review our definition of absolute value.

sections.title: Solve Absolute Value Inequalities with “Less Than”
sections.paragraph: Let’s look now at what happens when we have an absolute value inequality. Everything we’ve learned about solving inequalities still holds, but we must consider how the absolute value impacts our work.

sections.title: Solve Absolute Value Inequalities with “Greater Than”
sections.paragraph: What happens for absolute value inequalities that have “greater than”? Again we will look at our definition of absolute value. The absolute value of a number is its distance from zero on the number line.

sections.title: Solve Applications with Absolute Value
sections.paragraph: Absolute value inequalities are often used in the manufacturing process. An item must be made with near perfect specifications. Usually there is a certain *tolerance* of the difference from the specifications that is allowed. If the difference from the specifications exceeds the tolerance, the item is rejected.

chapters.title: Graph  Linear Equations in Two Variables
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Plot points in a rectangular coordinate system
* Graph a linear equation by plotting points
* Graph vertical and horizontal lines
* Find the x- and y-intercepts
* Graph a line using the intercepts

sections.title: Plot Points on a Rectangular Coordinate System
sections.paragraph: Just like maps use a grid system to identify locations, a grid system is used in algebra to show a relationship between two variables in a rectangular coordinate system. The rectangular coordinate system is also called the *xy*-plane or the “coordinate plane.”

sections.title: Graph a Linear Equation by Plotting Points
sections.paragraph: There are several methods that can be used to graph a linear equation. The first method we will use is called plotting points, or the Point-Plotting Method. We find three points whose coordinates are solutions to the equation and then plot them in a rectangular coordinate system. By connecting these points in a line, we have the graph of the linear equation.

sections.title: Graph Vertical and Horizontal Lines
sections.paragraph: Some linear equations have only one variable. They may have just *x* and no *y*, or just *y* without an *x*. This changes how we make a table of values to get the points to plot.

sections.title: Find *x*- and *y*-intercepts
sections.paragraph: Every linear equation can be represented by a unique line that shows all the solutions of the equation. We have seen that when graphing a line by plotting points, you can use any three solutions to graph. This means that two people graphing the line might use different sets of three points.

sections.title: Graph a Line Using the Intercepts
sections.paragraph: To graph a linear equation by plotting points, you need to find three points whose coordinates are solutions to the equation. You can use the *x-* and *y-* intercepts as two of your three points. Find the intercepts, and then find a third point to ensure accuracy. Make sure the points line up—then draw the line. This method is often the quickest way to graph a line.

chapters.title: Slope of a Line
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Find the slope of a line
* Graph a line given a point and the slope
* Graph a line using its slope and intercept
* Choose the most convenient method to graph a line
* Graph and interpret applications of slope–intercept
* Use slopes to identify parallel and perpendicular lines

sections.title: Find the Slope of a Line
sections.paragraph: When you graph linear equations, you may notice that some lines tilt up as they go from left to right and some lines tilt down. Some lines are very steep and some lines are flatter.

sections.title: Graph a Line Given a Point and the Slope
sections.paragraph: Up to now, in this chapter, we have graphed lines by plotting points, by using intercepts, and by recognizing horizontal and vertical lines.

sections.title: Graph a Line Using its Slope and Intercept
sections.paragraph: We have graphed linear equations by plotting points, using intercepts, recognizing horizontal and vertical lines, and using one point and the slope of the line. Once we see how an equation in slope–intercept form and its graph are related, we’ll have one more method we can use to graph lines.

sections.title: Choose the Most Convenient Method to Graph a Line
sections.paragraph: Now that we have seen several methods we can use to graph lines, how do we know which method to use for a given equation?

sections.title: Graph and Interpret Applications of Slope–Intercept
sections.paragraph: Many real-world applications are modeled by linear equations. We will take a look at a few applications here so you can see how equations written in slope–intercept form relate to real world situations.

sections.title: Use Slopes to Identify Parallel and Perpendicular Lines
sections.paragraph: Two lines that have the same slope are called parallel lines. Parallel lines have the same steepness and never intersect.

chapters.title: Find the Equation of a Line
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Find an equation of the line given the slope and $y\text{-intercept}$
* Find an equation of the line given the slope and a point
* Find an equation of the line given two points
* Find an equation of a line parallel to a given line
* Find an equation of a line perpendicular to a given line

sections.title: Find an Equation of the Line Given the Slope and *y*-Intercept
sections.paragraph: We can easily determine the slope and intercept of a line if the equation is written in slope-intercept form, $y=mx+b.$ Now we will do the reverse—we will start with the slope and *y*-intercept and use them to find the equation of the line.

sections.title: Find an Equation of the Line Given the Slope and a Point
sections.paragraph: Finding an equation of a line using the slope-intercept form of the equation works well when you are given the slope and *y*-intercept or when you read them off a graph. But what happens when you have another point instead of the *y*-intercept?

sections.title: Find an Equation of the Line Given Two Points
sections.paragraph: When real-world data is collected, a linear model can be created from two data points. In the next example we’ll see how to find an equation of a line when just two points are given.

sections.title: Find an Equation of a Line Parallel to a Given Line
sections.paragraph: Suppose we need to find an equation of a line that passes through a specific point and is parallel to a given line. We can use the fact that parallel lines have the same slope. So we will have a point and the slope—just what we need to use the point-slope equation.

sections.title: Find an Equation of a Line Perpendicular to a Given Line
sections.paragraph: Now, let’s consider perpendicular lines. Suppose we need to find a line passing through a specific point and which is perpendicular to a given line. We can use the fact that perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals. We will again use the point-slope equation, like we did with parallel lines.

chapters.title: Graph Linear Inequalities in Two Variables
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Verify solutions to an inequality in two variables.
* Recognize the relation between the solutions of an inequality and its graph.
* Graph linear inequalities in two variables
* Solve applications using linear inequalities in two variables

sections.title: Verify Solutions to an Inequality in Two Variables
sections.paragraph: Previously we learned to solve inequalities with only one variable. We will now learn about inequalities containing two variables. In particular we will look at **linear inequalities** in two variables which are very similar to linear equations in two variables.

sections.title: Recognize the Relation Between the Solutions of an Inequality and its Graph
sections.paragraph: Now, we will look at how the solutions of an inequality relate to its graph.

sections.title: Graph Linear Inequalities in Two Variables
sections.paragraph: Now that we know what the graph of a linear inequality looks like and how it relates to a boundary equation we can use this knowledge to graph a given linear inequality.

sections.title: Solve Applications using Linear Inequalities in Two Variables
sections.paragraph: Many fields use linear inequalities to model a problem. While our examples may be about simple situations, they give us an opportunity to build our skills and to get a feel for how they might be used.

chapters.title: Relations and Functions
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Find the domain and range of a relation
* Determine if a relation is a function
* Find the value of a function

sections.title: Find the Domain and Range of a Relation
sections.paragraph: As we go about our daily lives, we have many data items or quantities that are paired to our names. Our social security number, student ID number, email address, phone number and our birthday are matched to our name. There is a relationship between our name and each of those items.

sections.title: Determine if a Relation is a Function
sections.paragraph: A special type of relation, called a function, occurs extensively in mathematics. A function is a relation that assigns to each element in its domain exactly one element in the range. For each ordered pair in the relation, each *x*-value is matched with only one *y*-value.

sections.title: Find the Value of a Function
sections.paragraph: It is very convenient to name a function and most often we name it *f*, *g*, *h*, *F*, *G*, or *H*. In any function, for each *x*-value from the domain we get a corresponding *y*-value in the range. For the function *f*, we write this range value *y* as $f\left(x\right).$ This is called function notation and is read *f* of *x* or the value of *f* at *x*. In this case the parentheses does not indicate multiplication.

chapters.title: Graphs of Functions
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Use the vertical line test
* Identify graphs of basic functions
* Read information from a graph of a function

sections.title: Use the Vertical Line Test
sections.paragraph: In the last section we learned how to determine if a relation is a function. The relations we looked at were expressed as a set of ordered pairs, a mapping or an equation. We will now look at how to tell if a graph is that of a function.

sections.title: Identify Graphs of Basic Functions
sections.paragraph: We used the equation $y=2x-3$ and its graph as we developed the vertical line test. We said that the relation defined by the equation $y=2x-3$ is a function.

sections.title: Read Information from a Graph of a Function
sections.paragraph: In the sciences and business, data is often collected and then graphed. The graph is analyzed, information is obtained from the graph and then often predictions are made from the data.

chapters.title: Solve Systems of Linear Equations with Two Variables
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Determine whether an ordered pair is a solution of a system of equations
* Solve a system of linear equations by graphing
* Solve a system of equations by substitution
* Solve a system of equations by elimination
* Choose the most convenient method to solve a system of linear equations

sections.title: Determine Whether an Ordered Pair is a Solution of a System of Equations
sections.paragraph: In Solving Linear Equations, we learned how to solve linear equations with one variable. Now we will work with two or more linear equations grouped together, which is known as a system of linear equations.

sections.title: Solve a System of Linear Equations by Graphing
sections.paragraph: In this section, we will use three methods to solve a system of linear equations. The first method we’ll use is graphing.

sections.title: Solve a System of Equations by Substitution
sections.paragraph: We will now solve systems of linear equations by the substitution method.

sections.title: Solve a System of Equations by Elimination
sections.paragraph: We have solved systems of linear equations by graphing and by substitution. Graphing works well when the variable coefficients are small and the solution has integer values. Substitution works well when we can easily solve one equation for one of the variables and not have too many fractions in the resulting expression.

sections.title: Choose the Most Convenient Method to Solve a System of Linear Equations
sections.paragraph: When you solve a system of linear equations in in an application, you will not be told which method to use. You will need to make that decision yourself. So you’ll want to choose the method that is easiest to do and minimizes your chance of making mistakes.

chapters.title: Solve Applications with Systems of Equations
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve direct translation applications
* Solve geometry applications
* Solve uniform motion applications

sections.title: Solve Direct Translation Applications
sections.paragraph: Systems of linear equations are very useful for solving applications. Some people find setting up word problems with two variables easier than setting them up with just one variable. To solve an application, we’ll first translate the words into a system of linear equations. Then we will decide the most convenient method to use, and then solve the system.

sections.title: Solve Geometry Applications
sections.paragraph: We will now solve geometry applications using systems of linear equations. We will need to add complementary angles and supplementary angles to our list some properties of angles.

sections.title: Solve uniform motion applications
sections.paragraph: We used a table to organize the information in uniform motion problems when we introduced them earlier. We’ll continue using the table here. The basic equation was $D=rt$ where *D* is the distance traveled, *r* is the rate, and *t* is the time.

chapters.title: Solve Mixture Applications with Systems of Equations
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve mixture applications
* Solve interest applications
* Solve applications of cost and revenue functions

sections.title: Solve Mixture Applications
sections.paragraph: Mixture application involve combining two or more quantities. When we solved mixture applications with coins and tickets earlier, we started by creating a table so we could organize the information. For a coin example with nickels and dimes, the table looked like this:

sections.title: Solve Interest Applications
sections.paragraph: The formula to model simple interest applications is $I=Prt.$ Interest, *I*, is the product of the principal, *P*, the rate, *r*, and the time, *t*. In our work here, we will calculate the interest earned in one year, so *t* will be 1.

sections.title: Solve applications of cost and revenue functions
sections.paragraph: Suppose a company makes and sells *x* units of a product. The cost to the company is the total costs to produce *x* units. This is the cost to manufacture for each unit times *x*, the number of units manufactured, plus the fixed costs.

chapters.title: Solve Systems of Equations with Three Variables
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Determine whether an ordered triple is a solution of a system of three linear equations with three variables
* Solve a system of linear equations with three variables
* Solve applications using systems of linear equations with three variables

sections.title: Determine Whether an Ordered Triple is a Solution of a System of Three Linear Equations with Three Variables
sections.paragraph: In this section, we will extend our work of solving a system of linear equations. So far we have worked with systems of equations with two equations and two variables. Now we will work with systems of three equations with three variables. But first let's review what we already know about solving equations and systems involving up to two variables.

sections.title: Solve a System of Linear Equations with Three Variables
sections.paragraph: To solve a system of linear equations with three variables, we basically use the same techniques we used with systems that had two variables. We start with two pairs of equations and in each pair we eliminate the same variable. This will then give us a system of equations with only two variables and then we know how to solve that system!

sections.title: Solve Applications using Systems of Linear Equations with Three Variables
sections.paragraph: Applications that are modeled by a systems of equations can be solved using the same techniques we used to solve the systems. Many of the application are just extensions to three variables of the types we have solved earlier.

chapters.title: Solve Systems of Equations Using Matrices
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Write the augmented matrix for a system of equations
* Use row operations on a matrix
* Solve systems of equations using matrices

sections.title: Write the Augmented Matrix for a System of Equations
sections.paragraph: Solving a system of equations can be a tedious operation where a simple mistake can wreak havoc on finding the solution. An alternative method which uses the basic procedures of elimination but with notation that is simpler is available. The method involves using a matrix. A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns.

sections.title: Use Row Operations on a Matrix
sections.paragraph: Once a system of equations is in its augmented matrix form, we will perform operations on the rows that will lead us to the solution.

sections.title: Solve Systems of Equations Using Matrices
sections.paragraph: To solve a system of equations using matrices, we transform the augmented matrix into a matrix in row-echelon form using row operations. For a consistent and independent system of equations, its augmented matrix is in row-echelon form when to the left of the vertical line, each entry on the diagonal is a 1 and all entries below the diagonal are zeros.

chapters.title: Solve Systems of Equations Using Determinants
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Evaluate the determinant of a $2{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}×{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}2$ matrix
* Evaluate the determinant of a $3{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}×{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}3$ matrix
* Use Cramer’s Rule to solve systems of equations
* Solve applications using determinants

sections.title: Evaluate the Determinant of a $2{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}×{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}2$ Matrix
sections.paragraph: If a matrix has the same number of rows and columns, we call it a square matrix. Each square matrix has a real number associated with it called its determinant. To find the determinant of the square matrix $\left[\begin{array}{c}a{\rule{1.5em}{0ex}}b\hfill \\ c{\rule{1.5em}{0ex}}d\hfill \end{array}\right],$ we first write it as $|\begin{array}{c}a{\rule{1.5em}{0ex}}b\hfill \\ c{\rule{1.5em}{0ex}}d\hfill \end{array}|.$ To get the real number value of the determinant we subtract the products of the diagonals, as shown.

sections.title: Evaluate the Determinant of a $3{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}×{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}3$ Matrix
sections.paragraph: To evaluate the determinant of a $3{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}×{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}3$ matrix, we have to be able to evaluate the minor of an entry in the determinant. The minor of an entry is the $2{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}×{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}2$ determinant found by eliminating the row and column in the $3{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}×{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}3$ determinant that contains the entry.

sections.title: Use Cramer’s Rule to Solve Systems of Equations
sections.paragraph: Cramer’s Rule is a method of solving systems of equations using determinants. It can be derived by solving the general form of the systems of equations by elimination. Here we will demonstrate the rule for both systems of two equations with two variables and for systems of three equations with three variables.

sections.title: Solve Applications using Determinants
sections.paragraph: An interesting application of determinants allows us to test if points are collinear. Three points $\left({x}_{1},{y}_{1}\right),$ $\left({x}_{2},{y}_{2}\right)$ and $\left({x}_{3},{y}_{3}\right)$ are collinear if and only if the determinant below is zero.

chapters.title: Graphing Systems of Linear Inequalities
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Determine whether an ordered pair is a solution of a system of linear inequalities
* Solve a system of linear inequalities by graphing
* Solve applications of systems of inequalities

sections.title: Determine whether an ordered pair is a solution of a system of linear inequalities
sections.paragraph: The definition of a system of linear inequalities is very similar to the definition of a system of linear equations.

sections.title: Solve a System of Linear Inequalities by Graphing
sections.paragraph: The solution to a single linear inequality is the region on one side of the boundary line that contains all the points that make the inequality true. The solution to a system of two linear inequalities is a region that contains the solutions to both inequalities. To find this region, we will graph each inequality separately and then locate the region where they are both true. The solution is always shown as a graph.

sections.title: Solve Applications of Systems of Inequalities
sections.paragraph: The first thing we’ll need to do to solve applications of systems of inequalities is to translate each condition into an inequality. Then we graph the system, as we did above, to see the region that contains the solutions. Many situations will be realistic only if both variables are positive, so we add inequalities to the system as additional requirements.

chapters.title: Add and Subtract Polynomials
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Determine the degree of polynomials
* Add and subtract polynomials
* Evaluate a polynomial function for a given value
* Add and subtract polynomial functions

sections.title: Determine the Degree of Polynomials
sections.paragraph:
We have learned that a *term* is a constant or the product of a constant and one or more variables. A monomial is an algebraic expression with one term. When it is of the form $a{x}^{m},$ where *a* is a constant and *m* is a whole number, it is called a monomial in one variable. Some examples of monomials in one variable are
 $2x,5y,17z,$ and $4{y}^{2}$. Monomials can also have more than one variable such as 
 $5abc$ and $-4{a}^{2}{b}^{3}{c}^{2}.$

sections.title: Add and Subtract Polynomials
sections.paragraph: We have learned how to simplify expressions by combining like terms. Remember, like terms must have the same variables with the same exponent. Since monomials are terms, adding and subtracting monomials is the same as combining like terms. If the monomials are like terms, we just combine them by adding or subtracting the coefficients.

sections.title: Evaluate a Polynomial Function for a Given Value
sections.paragraph: A polynomial function is a function defined by a polynomial. For example, $f\left(x\right)={x}^{2}+5x+6$ and $g\left(x\right)=3x-4$ are polynomial functions, because ${x}^{2}+5x+6$ and $3x-4$ are polynomials.

sections.title: Add and Subtract Polynomial Functions
sections.paragraph: Just as polynomials can be added and subtracted, polynomial functions can also be added and subtracted.

chapters.title: Properties of Exponents and Scientific Notation
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Simplify expressions using the properties for exponents
* Use the definition of a negative exponent
* Use scientific notation

sections.title: Simplify Expressions Using the Properties for Exponents
sections.paragraph: Remember that an exponent indicates repeated multiplication of the same quantity. For example, in the expression ${a}^{m},$ the *exponent m* tells us how many times we use the *base a* as a factor.

sections.title: Use the Definition of a Negative Exponent
sections.paragraph: We saw that the Quotient Property for Exponents has two forms depending on whether the exponent is larger in the numerator or the denominator. What if we just subtract exponents regardless of which is larger?

sections.title: Use Scientific Notation
sections.paragraph: Working with very large or very small numbers can be awkward. Since our number system is base ten we can use powers of ten to rewrite very large or very small numbers to make them easier to work with. Consider the numbers 4,000 and 0.004.

chapters.title: Multiply Polynomials
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Multiply monomials
* Multiply a polynomial by a monomial
* Multiply a binomial by a binomial
* Multiply a polynomial by a polynomial
* Multiply special products
* Multiply polynomial functions

sections.title: Multiply Monomials
sections.paragraph: We are ready to perform operations on polynomials. Since monomials are algebraic expressions, we can use the properties of exponents to multiply monomials.

sections.title: Multiply a Polynomial by a Monomial
sections.paragraph: Multiplying a polynomial by a monomial is really just applying the Distributive Property.

sections.title: Multiply a Binomial by a Binomial
sections.paragraph: Just like there are different ways to represent multiplication of numbers, there are several methods that can be used to multiply a binomial times a binomial. We will start by using the Distributive Property.

sections.title: Multiply a Polynomial by a Polynomial
sections.paragraph: We have multiplied monomials by monomials, monomials by polynomials, and binomials by binomials. Now we’re ready to multiply a polynomial by a polynomial. Remember, FOIL will not work in this case, but we can use either the Distributive Property or the Vertical Method.

sections.title: Multiply Special Products
sections.paragraph: Mathematicians like to look for patterns that will make their work easier. A good example of this is squaring binomials. While you can always get the product by writing the binomial twice and multiplying them, there is less work to do if you learn to use a pattern. Let’s start by looking at three examples and look for a pattern.

sections.title: Multiply Polynomial Functions
sections.paragraph: Just as polynomials can be multiplied, polynomial functions can also be multiplied.

chapters.title: Dividing Polynomials
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Dividing monomials
* Dividing a polynomial by a monomial
* Dividing polynomials using long division
* Dividing polynomials using synthetic division
* Dividing polynomial functions
* Use the remainder and factor theorems

sections.title: Dividing Monomials
sections.paragraph: We are now familiar with all the properties of exponents and used them to multiply polynomials. Next, we’ll use these properties to divide monomials and polynomials.

sections.title: Divide a Polynomial by a Monomial
sections.paragraph: Now that we know how to divide a monomial by a monomial, the next procedure is to divide a polynomial of two or more terms by a monomial.

sections.title: Divide Polynomials Using Long Division
sections.paragraph: Divide a polynomial by a binomial, we follow a procedure very similar to long division of numbers. So let’s look carefully the steps we take when we divide a 3-digit number, 875, by a 2-digit number, 25.

sections.title: Divide Polynomials using Synthetic Division
sections.paragraph: As we have mentioned before, mathematicians like to find patterns to make their work easier. Since long division can be tedious, let’s look back at the long division we did in [link] and look for some patterns. We will use this as a basis for what is called synthetic division. The same problem in the synthetic division format is shown next.

sections.title: Divide Polynomial Functions
sections.paragraph: Just as polynomials can be divided, polynomial functions can also be divided.

sections.title: Use the Remainder and Factor Theorem
sections.paragraph: Let’s look at the division problems we have just worked that ended up with a remainder. They are summarized in the chart below. If we take the dividend from each division problem and use it to define a function, we get the functions shown in the chart. When the divisor is written as $x-c,$ the value of the function at $c,f\left(c\right),$ is the same as the remainder from the division problem.

chapters.title: Greatest Common Factor and Factor by Grouping
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Find the greatest common factor of two or more expressions
* Factor the greatest common factor from a polynomial
* Factor by grouping

sections.title: Find the Greatest Common Factor of Two or More Expressions
sections.paragraph: Earlier we multiplied factors together to get a product. Now, we will reverse this process; we will start with a product and then break it down into its factors. Splitting a product into factors is called factoring.

sections.title: Factor the Greatest Common Factor from a Polynomial
sections.paragraph: It is sometimes useful to represent a number as a product of factors, for example, 12 as $2·6$ or $3·4.$ In algebra, it can also be useful to represent a polynomial in factored form. We will start with a product, such as $3{x}^{2}+15x,$ and end with its factors, $3x\left(x+5\right).$ To do this we apply the Distributive Property “in reverse.”

sections.title: Factor by Grouping
sections.paragraph: Sometimes there is no common factor of all the terms of a polynomial. When there are four terms we separate the polynomial into two parts with two terms in each part. Then look for the GCF in each part. If the polynomial can be factored, you will find a common factor emerges from both parts. Not all polynomials can be factored. Just like some numbers are prime, some polynomials are prime.

chapters.title: Factor Trinomials
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Factor trinomials of the form ${x}^{2}+bx+c$
* Factor trinomials of the form $a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ using trial and error
* Factor trinomials of the form $a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ using the ‘ac’ method
* Factor using substitution

sections.title: Factor Trinomials of the Form ${x}^{2}+bx+c$
sections.paragraph: You have already learned how to multiply binomials using FOIL. Now you’ll need to “undo” this multiplication. To factor the trinomial means to start with the product, and end with the factors.

sections.title: Factor Trinomials of the form *ax*2 + *bx* + *c* using Trial and Error
sections.paragraph: Our next step is to factor trinomials whose leading coefficient is not 1, trinomials of the form $a{x}^{2}+bx+c.$

sections.title: Factor Trinomials of the Form $a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ using the “ac” Method
sections.paragraph: Another way to factor trinomials of the form $a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ is the “ac” method. (The “ac” method is sometimes called the grouping method.) The “ac” method is actually an extension of the methods you used in the last section to factor trinomials with leading coefficient one. This method is very structured (that is step-by-step), and it always works!

sections.title: Factor Using Substitution
sections.paragraph: Sometimes a trinomial does not appear to be in the $a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ form. However, we can often make a thoughtful substitution that will allow us to make it fit the $a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ form. This is called factoring by substitution. It is standard to use *u* for the substitution.

chapters.title: Factor Special Products
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Factor perfect square trinomials
* Factor differences of squares
* Factor sums and differences of cubes

sections.title: Factor Perfect Square Trinomials
sections.paragraph: Some trinomials are perfect squares. They result from multiplying a binomial times itself. We squared a binomial using the Binomial Squares pattern in a previous chapter.

sections.title: Factor Differences of Squares
sections.paragraph: The other special product you saw in the previous chapter was the Product of Conjugates pattern. You used this to multiply two binomials that were conjugates. Here’s an example:

sections.title: Factor Sums and Differences of Cubes
sections.paragraph: There is another special pattern for factoring, one that we did not use when we multiplied polynomials. This is the pattern for the sum and difference of cubes. We will write these formulas first and then check them by multiplication.

chapters.title: General Strategy for Factoring Polynomials
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Recognize and use the appropriate method to factor a polynomial completely

sections.title: Recognize and Use the Appropriate Method to Factor a Polynomial Completely
sections.paragraph: You have now become acquainted with all the methods of factoring that you will need in this course. The following chart summarizes all the factoring methods we have covered, and outlines a strategy you should use when factoring polynomials.

chapters.title: Polynomial Equations
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Use the Zero Product Property
* Solve quadratic equations by factoring
* Solve equations with polynomial functions
* Solve applications modeled by polynomial equations

sections.title: Use the Zero Product Property
sections.paragraph: We will first solve some quadratic equations by using the Zero Product Property. The Zero Product Property says that if the product of two quantities is zero, then at least one of the quantities is zero. The only way to get a product equal to zero is to multiply by zero itself.

sections.title: Solve Quadratic Equations by Factoring
sections.paragraph: The Zero Product Property works very nicely to solve quadratic equations. The quadratic equation must be factored, with zero isolated on one side. So we must be sure to start with the quadratic equation in standard form, $a{x}^{2}+bx+c=0.$ Then we must factor the expression on the left.
