sections.title: Solve Equations with Polynomial Functions
sections.paragraph: As our study of polynomial functions continues, it will often be important to know when the function will have a certain value or what points lie on the graph of the function. Our work with the Zero Product Property will be help us find these answers.

sections.title: Solve Applications Modeled by Polynomial Equations
sections.paragraph: The problem-solving strategy we used earlier for applications that translate to linear equations will work just as well for applications that translate to polynomial equations. We will copy the problem-solving strategy here so we can use it for reference.

chapters.title: Multiply and Divide Rational Expressions
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Determine the values for which a rational expression is undefined
* Simplify rational expressions
* Multiply rational expressions
* Divide rational expressions
* Multiply and divide rational functions

sections.title: Determine the Values for Which a Rational Expression is Undefined
sections.paragraph: If the denominator is zero, the rational expression is undefined. The numerator of a rational expression may be 0—but not the denominator.

sections.title: Simplify Rational Expressions
sections.paragraph: A fraction is considered simplified if there are no common factors, other than 1, in its numerator and denominator. Similarly, a simplified rational expression has no common factors, other than 1, in its numerator and denominator.

sections.title: Multiply Rational Expressions
sections.paragraph: To multiply rational expressions, we do just what we did with numerical fractions. We multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators. Then, if there are any common factors, we remove them to simplify the result.

sections.title: Divide Rational Expressions
sections.paragraph: Just like we did for numerical fractions, to divide rational expressions, we multiply the first fraction by the reciprocal of the second.

sections.title: Multiply and Divide Rational Functions
sections.paragraph: We started this section stating that a rational expression is an expression of the form $\frac{p}{q},$ where *p* and *q* are polynomials and $q\ne 0.$ Similarly, we define a rational function as a function of the form $R\left(x\right)=\frac{p\left(x\right)}{q\left(x\right)}$ where $p\left(x\right)$ and $q\left(x\right)$ are polynomial functions and $q\left(x\right)$ is not zero.

chapters.title: Add and Subtract Rational Expressions
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Add and subtract rational expressions with a common denominator
* Add and subtract rational expressions whose denominators are opposites
* Find the least common denominator of rational expressions
* Add and subtract rational expressions with unlike denominators
* Add and subtract rational functions

sections.title: Add and Subtract Rational Expressions with a Common Denominator
sections.paragraph: What is the first step you take when you add numerical fractions? You check if they have a common denominator. If they do, you add the numerators and place the sum over the common denominator. If they do not have a common denominator, you find one before you add.

sections.title: Add and Subtract Rational Expressions Whose Denominators are Opposites
sections.paragraph: When the denominators of two rational expressions are opposites, it is easy to get a common denominator. We just have to multiply one of the fractions by $\frac{-1}{-1}.$

sections.title: Find the Least Common Denominator of Rational Expressions
sections.paragraph: When we add or subtract rational expressions with unlike denominators, we will need to get common denominators. If we review the procedure we used with numerical fractions, we will know what to do with rational expressions.

sections.title: Add and Subtract Rational Expressions with Unlike Denominators
sections.paragraph: Now we have all the steps we need to add or subtract rational expressions with unlike denominators.

sections.title: Add and subtract rational functions
sections.paragraph: To add or subtract rational functions, we use the same techniques we used to add or subtract polynomial functions.

chapters.title: Simplify Complex Rational Expressions
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Simplify a complex rational expression by writing it as division
* Simplify a complex rational expression by using the LCD

sections.title: Simplify a Complex Rational Expression by Writing it as Division
sections.paragraph: Complex fractions are fractions in which the numerator or denominator contains a fraction. We previously simplified complex fractions like these:

sections.title: Simplify a Complex Rational Expression by Using the LCD
sections.paragraph: We “cleared” the fractions by multiplying by the LCD when we solved equations with fractions. We can use that strategy here to simplify complex rational expressions. We will multiply the numerator and denominator by the LCD of all the rational expressions.

chapters.title: Solve Rational Equations
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve rational equations
* Use rational functions
* Solve a rational equation for a specific variable

sections.title: Solve Rational Equations
sections.paragraph: We have already solved linear equations that contained fractions. We found the LCD of all the fractions in the equation and then multiplied both sides of the equation by the LCD to “clear” the fractions.

sections.title: Use Rational Functions
sections.paragraph: Working with functions that are defined by rational expressions often lead to rational equations. Again, we use the same techniques to solve them.

sections.title: Solve a Rational Equation for a Specific Variable
sections.paragraph: When we solved linear equations, we learned how to solve a formula for a specific variable. Many formulas used in business, science, economics, and other fields use rational equations to model the relation between two or more variables. We will now see how to solve a rational equation for a specific variable.

chapters.title: Solve Applications with Rational Equations
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve proportions
* Solve similar figure applications
* Solve uniform motion applications
* Solve work applications
* Solve direct variation problems
* Solve inverse variation problems

sections.title: Solve Proportions
sections.paragraph: When two rational expressions are equal, the equation relating them is called a proportion.

sections.title: Solve similar figure applications
sections.paragraph: When you shrink or enlarge a photo on a phone or tablet, figure out a distance on a map, or use a pattern to build a bookcase or sew a dress, you are working with similar figures. If two figures have exactly the same shape, but different sizes, they are said to be similar. One is a scale model of the other. All their corresponding angles have the same measures and their corresponding sides have the same ratio.

sections.title: Solve Uniform Motion Applications
sections.paragraph: We have solved uniform motion problems using the formula $D=rt$ in previous chapters. We used a table like the one below to organize the information and lead us to the equation.

sections.title: Solve Work Applications
sections.paragraph: The weekly gossip magazine has a big story about the Princess’ baby and the editor wants the magazine to be printed as soon as possible. She has asked the printer to run an extra printing press to get the printing done more quickly. Press #1 takes 6 hours to do the job and Press #2 takes 12 hours to do the job. How long will it take the printer to get the magazine printed with both presses running together?

sections.title: Solve Direct Variation Problems
sections.paragraph: When two quantities are related by a proportion, we say they are *proportional* to each other. Another way to express this relation is to talk about the *variation* of the two quantities. We will discuss direct variation and inverse variation in this section.

sections.title: Solve Inverse Variation Problems
sections.paragraph: Many applications involve two variable that *vary inversely*. As one variable increases, the other decreases. The equation that relates them is $y=\frac{k}{x}.$

chapters.title: Solve Rational Inequalities
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve rational inequalities
* Solve an inequality with rational functions

sections.title: Solve Rational Inequalities
sections.paragraph: We learned to solve linear inequalities after learning to solve linear equations. The techniques were very much the same with one major exception. When we multiplied or divided by a negative number, the inequality sign reversed.

sections.title: Solve an Inequality with Rational Functions
sections.paragraph: When working with rational functions, it is sometimes useful to know when the function is greater than or less than a particular value. This leads to a rational inequality.

chapters.title: Simplify Expressions with Roots
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Simplify expressions with roots
* Estimate and approximate roots
* Simplify variable expressions with roots

sections.title: Simplify Expressions with Roots
sections.paragraph: In Foundations, we briefly looked at square roots. Remember that when a real number *n* is multiplied by itself, we write ${n}^{2}$ and read it ‘*n* squared’. This number is called the square of *n*, and *n* is called the square root. For example,

sections.title: Estimate and Approximate Roots
sections.paragraph: When we see a number with a radical sign, we often don’t think about its numerical value. While we probably know that the $\sqrt{4}=2,$ what is the value of $\sqrt[]{21}$ or $\sqrt[3]{50}?$ In some situations a quick estimate is meaningful and in others it is convenient to have a decimal approximation.

sections.title: Simplify Variable Expressions with Roots
sections.paragraph: The odd root of a number can be either positive or negative. For example,

chapters.title: Simplify Radical Expressions
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Use the Product Property to simplify radical expressions
* Use the Quotient Property to simplify radical expressions

sections.title: Use the Product Property to Simplify Radical Expressions
sections.paragraph: We will simplify radical expressions in a way similar to how we simplified fractions. A fraction is simplified if there are no common factors in the numerator and denominator. To simplify a fraction, we look for any common factors in the numerator and denominator.

sections.title: Use the Quotient Property to Simplify Radical Expressions
sections.paragraph: Whenever you have to simplify a radical expression, the first step you should take is to determine whether the radicand is a perfect power of the index. If not, check the numerator and denominator for any common factors, and remove them. You may find a fraction in which both the numerator and the denominator are perfect powers of the index.

chapters.title: Simplify Rational Exponents
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Simplify expressions with ${a}^{\frac{1}{n}}$
* Simplify expressions with ${a}^{\frac{m}{n}}$
* Use the properties of exponents to simplify expressions with rational exponents

sections.title: Simplify Expressions with ${a}^{\frac{1}{n}}$
sections.paragraph: Rational exponents are another way of writing expressions with radicals. When we use rational exponents, we can apply the properties of exponents to simplify expressions.

sections.title: Simplify Expressions with ${a}^{\frac{m}{n}}$
sections.paragraph: We can look at ${a}^{\frac{m}{n}}$ in two ways. Remember the Power Property tells us to multiply the exponents and so ${\left({a}^{\frac{1}{n}}\right)}^{m}$ and ${\left({a}^{m}\right)}^{{}^{\frac{1}{n}}}$ both equal ${a}^{\frac{m}{n}}.$ If we write these expressions in radical form, we get

sections.title: Use the Properties of Exponents to Simplify Expressions with Rational Exponents
sections.paragraph: The same properties of exponents that we have already used also apply to rational exponents. We will list the Properties of Exponenets here to have them for reference as we simplify expressions.

chapters.title: Add, Subtract, and Multiply Radical Expressions
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Add and subtract radical expressions
* Multiply radical expressions
* Use polynomial multiplication to multiply radical expressions

sections.title: Add and Subtract Radical Expressions
sections.paragraph: Adding radical expressions with the same index and the same radicand is just like adding like terms. We call radicals with the same index and the same radicand like radicals to remind us they work the same as like terms.

sections.title: Multiply Radical Expressions
sections.paragraph: We have used the Product Property of Roots to simplify square roots by removing the perfect square factors. We can use the Product Property of Roots ‘in reverse’ to multiply square roots. Remember, we assume all variables are greater than or equal to zero.

sections.title: Use Polynomial Multiplication to Multiply Radical Expressions
sections.paragraph: In the next a few examples, we will use the Distributive Property to multiply expressions with radicals. First we will distribute and then simplify the radicals when possible.

chapters.title: Divide Radical Expressions
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Divide radical expressions
* Rationalize a one term denominator
* Rationalize a two term denominator

sections.title: Divide Radical Expressions
sections.paragraph: We have used the Quotient Property of Radical Expressions to simplify roots of fractions. We will need to use this property ‘in reverse’ to simplify a fraction with radicals.

sections.title: Rationalize a One Term Denominator
sections.paragraph: Before the calculator became a tool of everyday life, approximating the value of a fraction with a radical in the denominator was a very cumbersome process!

sections.title: Rationalize a Two Term Denominator
sections.paragraph: When the denominator of a fraction is a sum or difference with square roots, we use the Product of Conjugates Pattern to rationalize the denominator.

chapters.title: Solve Radical Equations
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve radical equations
* Solve radical equations with two radicals
* Use radicals in applications

sections.title: Solve Radical Equations
sections.paragraph: In this section we will solve equations that have a variable in the radicand of a radical expression. An equation of this type is called a radical equation.

sections.title: Solve Radical Equations with Two Radicals
sections.paragraph: If the radical equation has two radicals, we start out by isolating one of them. It often works out easiest to isolate the more complicated radical first.

sections.title: Use Radicals in Applications
sections.paragraph: As you progress through your college courses, you’ll encounter formulas that include radicals in many disciplines. We will modify our Problem Solving Strategy for Geometry Applications slightly to give us a plan for solving applications with formulas from any discipline.

chapters.title: Use Radicals in Functions
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Evaluate a radical function
* Find the domain of a radical function
* Graph radical functions

sections.title: Evaluate a Radical Function
sections.paragraph: In this section we will extend our previous work with functions to include radicals. If a function is defined by a radical expression, we call it a radical function.

sections.title: Find the Domain of a Radical Function
sections.paragraph: To find the domain and range of radical functions, we use our properties of radicals. For a radical with an even index, we said the radicand had to be greater than or equal to zero as even roots of negative numbers are not real numbers. For an odd index, the radicand can be any real number. We restate the properties here for reference.

sections.title: Graph Radical Functions
sections.paragraph: Before we graph any radical function, we first find the domain of the function. For the function, $f\left(x\right)=\sqrt{x},$ the index is even, and so the radicand must be greater than or equal to 0.

chapters.title: Use the Complex Number System
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Evaluate the square root of a negative number
* Add and subtract complex numbers
* Multiply complex numbers
* Divide complex numbers
* Simplify powers of $i$

sections.title: Evaluate the Square Root of a Negative Number
sections.paragraph: Whenever we have a situation where we have a square root of a negative number we say there is no real number that equals that square root. For example, to simplify $\sqrt{-1},$ we are looking for a real number *x* so that *x*2 = –1. Since all real numbers squared are positive numbers, there is no real number that equals –1 when squared.

sections.title: Add or Subtract Complex Numbers
sections.paragraph: We are now ready to perform the operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication and division on the complex numbers—just as we did with the real numbers.

sections.title: Multiply Complex Numbers
sections.paragraph: Multiplying complex numbers is also much like multiplying expressions with coefficients and variables. There is only one special case we need to consider. We will look at that after we practice in the next two examples.

sections.title: Divide Complex Numbers
sections.paragraph: Dividing complex numbers is much like rationalizing a denominator. We want our result to be in standard form with no imaginary numbers in the denominator.

sections.title: Simplify Powers of *i*
sections.paragraph: The powers of $i$ make an interesting pattern that will help us simplify higher powers of *i*. Let’s evaluate the powers of $i$ to see the pattern.

chapters.title: Solve Quadratic Equations Using the Square Root Property
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve quadratic equations of the form ${ax}^{2}=k$ using the Square Root Property
* Solve quadratic equations of the form $a{\left(x–h\right)}^{2}=k$ using the Square Root Property

sections.title: Solve Quadratic Equations of the form $a{x}^{2}=k$ using the Square Root Property
sections.paragraph: We have already solved some quadratic equations by factoring. Let’s review how we used factoring to solve the quadratic equation *x*2 = 9.

sections.title: Solve Quadratic Equations of the Form *a*(*x* − *h*)2 = *k* Using the Square Root Property
sections.paragraph: We can use the Square Root Property to solve an equation of the form *a*(*x* − *h*)2 = *k* as well. Notice that the quadratic term, *x*, in the original form *ax*2 = *k* is replaced with (*x* − *h*).

chapters.title: Solve Quadratic Equations by Completing the Square
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Complete the square of a binomial expression
* Solve quadratic equations of the form ${x}^{2}+bx+c=0$ by completing the square
* Solve quadratic equations of the form ${ax}^{2}+bx+c=0$ by completing the square

sections.title: Complete the Square of a Binomial Expression
sections.paragraph: In the last section, we were able to use the Square Root Property to solve the equation (*y* − 7)2 = 12 because the left side was a perfect square.

sections.title: Solve Quadratic Equations of the Form *x*2 + *bx* + *c* = 0 by Completing the Square
sections.paragraph: In solving equations, we must always do the same thing to both sides of the equation. This is true, of course, when we solve a quadratic equation by completing the square too. When we add a term to one side of the equation to make a perfect square trinomial, we must also add the same term to the other side of the equation.

sections.title: Solve Quadratic Equations of the Form *ax*2 + *bx* + *c* = 0 by Completing the Square
sections.paragraph: The process of completing the square works best when the coefficient of *x*2 is 1, so the left side of the equation is of the form *x*2 + *bx* + *c*. If the *x*2 term has a coefficient other than 1, we take some preliminary steps to make the coefficient equal to 1.

chapters.title: Solve Quadratic Equations Using the Quadratic Formula
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve quadratic equations using the Quadratic Formula
* Use the discriminant to predict the number and type of solutions of a quadratic equation
* Identify the most appropriate method to use to solve a quadratic equation

sections.title: Solve Quadratic Equations Using the Quadratic Formula
sections.paragraph: When we solved quadratic equations in the last section by completing the square, we took the same steps every time. By the end of the exercise set, you may have been wondering ‘isn’t there an easier way to do this?’ The answer is ‘yes’. Mathematicians look for patterns when they do things over and over in order to make their work easier. In this section we will derive and use a formula to find the solution of a quadratic equation.

sections.title: Use the Discriminant to Predict the Number and Type of Solutions of a Quadratic Equation
sections.paragraph: When we solved the quadratic equations in the previous examples, sometimes we got two real solutions, one real solution, and sometimes two complex solutions. Is there a way to predict the number and type of solutions to a quadratic equation without actually solving the equation?

sections.title: Identify the Most Appropriate Method to Use to Solve a Quadratic Equation
sections.paragraph: We summarize the four methods that we have used to solve quadratic equations below.

chapters.title: Solve Equations in Quadratic Form
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve equations in quadratic form

sections.title: Solve Equations in Quadratic Form
sections.paragraph: Sometimes when we factored trinomials, the trinomial did not appear to be in the *ax*2 + *bx* + *c* form. So we factored by substitution allowing us to make it fit the *ax*2 + *bx* + *c* form. We used the standard $u$ for the substitution.

chapters.title: Solve Applications of Quadratic Equations
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve applications modeled by quadratic equations

sections.title: Solve Applications Modeled by Quadratic Equations
sections.paragraph: We solved some applications that are modeled by quadratic equations earlier, when the only method we had to solve them was factoring. Now that we have more methods to solve quadratic equations, we will take another look at applications.

chapters.title: Graph Quadratic Functions Using Properties
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Recognize the graph of a quadratic function
* Find the axis of symmetry and vertex of a parabola
* Find the intercepts of a parabola
* Graph quadratic functions using properties
* Solve maximum and minimum applications

sections.title: Recognize the Graph of a Quadratic Function
sections.paragraph: Previously we very briefly looked at the function $f\left(x\right)={x}^{2}$, which we called the square function. It was one of the first non-linear functions we looked at. Now we will graph functions of the form $f\left(x\right)=a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ if $a\ne 0.$ We call this kind of function a quadratic function.

sections.title: Find the Axis of Symmetry and Vertex of a Parabola
sections.paragraph: Look again at [link]. Do you see that we could fold each parabola in half and then one side would lie on top of the other? The ‘fold line’ is a line of symmetry. We call it the axis of symmetry of the parabola.

sections.title: Find the Intercepts of a Parabola
sections.paragraph: When we graphed linear equations, we often used the *x*- and *y*-intercepts to help us graph the lines. Finding the coordinates of the intercepts will help us to graph parabolas, too.

sections.title: Graph Quadratic Functions Using Properties
sections.paragraph: Now we have all the pieces we need in order to graph a quadratic function. We just need to put them together. In the next example we will see how to do this.

sections.title: Solve Maximum and Minimum Applications
sections.paragraph: Knowing that the vertex of a parabola is the lowest or highest point of the parabola gives us an easy way to determine the minimum or maximum value of a quadratic function. The *y*-coordinate of the vertex is the minimum value of a parabola that opens upward. It is the maximum value of a parabola that opens downward. See [link].

chapters.title: Graph Quadratic Functions Using Transformations
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Graph quadratic equations of the form $f\left(x\right)={x}^{2}+k$
* Graph quadratic functions of the form $f\left(x\right)={\left(x-h\right)}^{2}$
* Graph quadratic functions of the form $f\left(x\right)=a{x}^{2}$
* Graph quadratic functions using transformations
* Find a quadratic function from its graph

sections.title: Graph Quadratic Functions of the form $f\left(x\right)={x}^{2}+k$
sections.paragraph: In the last section, we learned how to graph quadratic functions using their properties. Another method involves starting with the basic graph of $f\left(x\right)={x}^{2}$ and ‘moving’ it according to information given in the function equation. We call this graphing quadratic functions using transformations.

sections.title: Graph Quadratic Functions of the form $f\left(x\right)={\left(x-h\right)}^{2}$
sections.paragraph: In the first example, we graphed the quadratic function $f\left(x\right)={x}^{2}$ by plotting points and then saw the effect of adding a constant *k* to the function had on the resulting graph of the new function $f\left(x\right)={x}^{2}+k.$

sections.title: Graph Quadratic Functions of the Form $f\left(x\right)=a{x}^{2}$
sections.paragraph: So far we graphed the quadratic function $f\left(x\right)={x}^{2}$ and then saw the effect of including a constant *h* or *k* in the equation had on the resulting graph of the new function. We will now explore the effect of the coefficient *a* on the resulting graph of the new function $f\left(x\right)=a{x}^{2}.$

sections.title: Graph Quadratic Functions Using Transformations
sections.paragraph: We have learned how the constants *a*, *h*, and *k* in the functions, $f\left(x\right)={x}^{2}+k,{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}f\left(x\right)={\left(x-h\right)}^{2},$ and $f\left(x\right)=a{x}^{2}$ affect their graphs. We can now put this together and graph quadratic functions $f\left(x\right)=a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ by first putting them into the form $f\left(x\right)=a{\left(x-h\right)}^{2}+k$ by completing the square. This form is sometimes known as the vertex form or standard form.

sections.title: Find a Quadratic Function from its Graph
sections.paragraph: So far we have started with a function and then found its graph.

chapters.title: Solve Quadratic Inequalities
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve quadratic inequalities graphically
* Solve quadratic inequalities algebraically

sections.title: Solve Quadratic Inequalities Graphically
sections.paragraph: A quadratic equation is in standard form when written as *ax*2 + *bx* + *c* = 0. If we replace the equal sign with an inequality sign, we have a quadratic inequality in standard form.

sections.title: Solve Quadratic Inequalities Algebraically
sections.paragraph: The algebraic method we will use is very similar to the method we used to solve rational inequalities. We will find the critical points for the inequality, which will be the solutions to the related quadratic equation. Remember a polynomial expression can change signs only where the expression is zero.

chapters.title: Finding Composite and Inverse Functions
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Find and evaluate composite functions
* Determine whether a function is one-to-one
* Find the inverse of a function

sections.title: Find and Evaluate Composite Functions
sections.paragraph: Before we introduce the functions, we need to look at another operation on functions called composition. In composition, the output of one function is the input of a second function. For functions $f$ and $g,$ the composition is written $f\circ g$ and is defined by $\left(f\circ g\right)\left(x\right)=f\left(g\left(x\right)\right).$

sections.title: Determine Whether a Function is One-to-One
sections.paragraph: When we first introduced functions, we said a function is a relation that assigns to each element in its domain exactly one element in the range. For each ordered pair in the relation, each *x*-value is matched with only one *y*-value.

sections.title: Find the Inverse of a Function
sections.paragraph: Let’s look at a one-to one function, $f$, represented by the ordered pairs $\left\{\left(0,5\right),\left(1,6\right),\left(2,7\right),\left(3,8\right)\right\}.$ For each $x$-value, $f$ adds 5 to get the $y$-value. To ‘undo’ the addition of 5, we subtract 5 from each $y$-value and get back to the original $x$-value. We can call this “taking the inverse of $f$” and name the function ${f}^{-1}.$

chapters.title: Evaluate and Graph Exponential Functions
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Graph exponential functions
* Solve Exponential equations
* Use exponential models in applications

sections.title: Graph Exponential Functions
sections.paragraph: The functions we have studied so far do not give us a model for many naturally occurring phenomena. From the growth of populations and the spread of viruses to radioactive decay and compounding interest, the models are very different from what we have studied so far. These models involve exponential functions.

sections.title: Solve Exponential Equations
sections.paragraph: Equations that include an exponential expression ${a}^{x}$ are called exponential equations. To solve them we use a property that says as long as $a>0$ and $a\ne 1,$ if ${a}^{x}={a}^{y}$ then it is true that $x=y.$ In other words, in an exponential equation, if the bases are equal then the exponents are equal.

sections.title: Use Exponential Models in Applications
sections.paragraph: Exponential functions model many situations. If you own a bank account, you have experienced the use of an exponential function. There are two formulas that are used to determine the balance in the account when interest is earned. If a principal, *P*, is invested at an interest rate, *r*, for *t* years, the new balance, *A*, will depend on how often the interest is compounded. If the interest is compounded *n* times a year we use the formula $A=P{\left(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)}^{nt}.$ If the interest is compounded continuously, we use the formula $A=P{e}^{rt}.$ These are the formulas for compound interest.

chapters.title: Evaluate and Graph Logarithmic Functions
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Convert between exponential and logarithmic form
* Evaluate logarithmic functions
* Graph Logarithmic functions
* Solve logarithmic equations
* Use logarithmic models in applications

sections.title: Convert Between Exponential and Logarithmic Form
sections.paragraph: Since the equations $y={\text{log}}_{a}x$ and $x={a}^{y}$ are equivalent, we can go back and forth between them. This will often be the method to solve some exponential and logarithmic equations. To help with converting back and forth let’s take a close look at the equations. See [link]. Notice the positions of the exponent and base.

sections.title: Evaluate Logarithmic Functions
sections.paragraph: We can solve and evaluate logarithmic equations by using the technique of converting the equation to its equivalent exponential equation.

sections.title: Graph Logarithmic Functions
sections.paragraph: To graph a logarithmic function $y={\text{log}}_{a}x,$ it is easiest to convert the equation to its exponential form, $x={a}^{y}.$ Generally, when we look for ordered pairs for the graph of a function, we usually choose an *x*-value and then determine its corresponding *y*-value. In this case you may find it easier to choose *y*-values and then determine its corresponding *x*-value.

sections.title: Solve Logarithmic Equations
sections.paragraph: When we talked about exponential functions, we introduced the number *e*. Just as *e* was a base for an exponential function, it can be used a base for logarithmic functions too. The logarithmic function with base *e* is called the natural logarithmic function. The function $f\left(x\right)={\text{log}}_{e}x$ is generally written $f\left(x\right)=\text{ln}{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}x$ and we read it as “el en of $x.”$

sections.title: Use Logarithmic Models in Applications
sections.paragraph: There are many applications that are modeled by logarithmic equations. We will first look at the logarithmic equation that gives the decibel (dB) level of sound. Decibels range from 0, which is barely audible to 160, which can rupture an eardrum. The ${10}^{-12}$ in the formula represents the intensity of sound that is barely audible.

chapters.title: Use the Properties of Logarithms
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Use the properties of logarithms
* Use the Change of Base Formula

sections.title: Use the Properties of Logarithms
sections.paragraph: Now that we have learned about exponential and logarithmic functions, we can introduce some of the properties of logarithms. These will be very helpful as we continue to solve both exponential and logarithmic equations.

sections.title: Use the Change-of-Base Formula
sections.paragraph: To evaluate a logarithm with any other base, we can use the Change-of-Base Formula. We will show how this is derived.

chapters.title: Solve Exponential and Logarithmic Equations
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve logarithmic equations using the properties of logarithms
* Solve exponential equations using logarithms
* Use exponential models in applications

sections.title: Solve Logarithmic Equations Using the Properties of Logarithms
sections.paragraph: In the section on logarithmic functions, we solved some equations by rewriting the equation in exponential form. Now that we have the properties of logarithms, we have additional methods we can use to solve logarithmic equations.

sections.title: Solve Exponential Equations Using Logarithms
sections.paragraph: In the section on exponential functions, we solved some equations by writing both sides of the equation with the same base. Next we wrote a new equation by setting the exponents equal.

sections.title: Use Exponential Models in Applications
sections.paragraph: In previous sections we were able to solve some applications that were modeled with exponential equations. Now that we have so many more options to solve these equations, we are able to solve more applications.

chapters.title: Distance and Midpoint Formulas; Circles
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Use the Distance Formula
* Use the Midpoint Formula
* Write the equation of a circle in standard form
* Graph a circle

sections.title: Use the Distance Formula
sections.paragraph: We have used the Pythagorean Theorem to find the lengths of the sides of a right triangle. Here we will use this theorem again to find distances on the rectangular coordinate system. By finding distance on the rectangular coordinate system, we can make a connection between the geometry of a conic and algebra—which opens up a world of opportunities for application.

sections.title: Use the Midpoint Formula
sections.paragraph: It is often useful to be able to find the midpoint of a segment. For example, if you have the endpoints of the diameter of a circle, you may want to find the center of the circle which is the midpoint of the diameter. To find the midpoint of a line segment, we find the average of the *x*-coordinates and the average of the *y*-coordinates of the endpoints.

sections.title: Write the Equation of a Circle in Standard Form
sections.paragraph: As we mentioned, our goal is to connect the geometry of a conic with algebra. By using the coordinate plane, we are able to do this easily.

sections.title: Graph a Circle
sections.paragraph: Any equation of the form ${\left(x-h\right)}^{2}+{\left(y-k\right)}^{2}={r}^{2}$ is the standard form of the equation of a circle with center, $\left(h,k\right),$ and radius, *r.* We can then graph the circle on a rectangular coordinate system.

chapters.title: Parabolas
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Graph vertical parabolas
* Graph horizontal parabolas
* Solve applications with parabolas

sections.title: Graph Vertical Parabolas
sections.paragraph: The next conic section we will look at is a parabola. We define a parabola as all points in a plane that are the same distance from a fixed point and a fixed line. The fixed point is called the **focus,** and the fixed line is called the **directrix** of the parabola.

sections.title: Graph Horizontal Parabolas
sections.paragraph: Our work so far has only dealt with parabolas that open up or down. We are now going to look at horizontal parabolas. These parabolas open either to the left or to the right. If we interchange the *x* and *y* in our previous equations for parabolas, we get the equations for the parabolas that open to the left or to the right.

sections.title: Solve Applications with Parabolas
sections.paragraph: Many architectural designs incorporate parabolas. It is not uncommon for bridges to be constructed using parabolas as we will see in the next example.

chapters.title: Ellipses
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Graph an ellipse with center at the origin
* Find the equation of an ellipse with center at the origin
* Graph an ellipse with center not at the origin
* Solve application with ellipses

sections.title: Graph an Ellipse with Center at the Origin
sections.paragraph: The next conic section we will look at is an ellipse. We define an ellipse as all points in a plane where the sum of the distances from two fixed points is constant. Each of the given points is called a **focus** of the ellipse.

sections.title: Find the Equation of an Ellipse with Center at the Origin
sections.paragraph: If we are given the graph of an ellipse, we can find the equation of the ellipse.

sections.title: Graph an Ellipse with Center Not at the Origin
sections.paragraph: The ellipses we have looked at so far have all been centered at the origin. We will now look at ellipses whose center is $\left(h,k\right).$

chapters.title: Hyperbolas
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Graph a hyperbola with center at $\left(0,0\right)$
* Graph a hyperbola with center at $\left(h,k\right)$
* Identify conic sections by their equations

sections.title: Graph a Hyperbola with Center at **(0, 0)**
sections.paragraph: The last conic section we will look at is called a hyperbola. We will see that the equation of a hyperbola looks the same as the equation of an ellipse, except it is a difference rather than a sum. While the equations of an ellipse and a hyperbola are very similar, their graphs are very different.

sections.title: Graph a Hyperbola with Center at $\left(h,k\right)$
sections.paragraph: Hyperbolas are not always centered at the origin. When a hyperbola is centered at $\left(h,k\right)$ the equations changes a bit as reflected in the table.

sections.title: Identify Conic Sections by their Equations
sections.paragraph: Now that we have completed our study of the conic sections, we will take a look at the different equations and recognize some ways to identify a conic by its equation. When we are given an equation to graph, it is helpful to identify the conic so we know what next steps to take.

chapters.title: Solve Systems of Nonlinear Equations
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Solve a system of nonlinear equations using graphing
* Solve a system of nonlinear equations using substitution
* Solve a system of nonlinear equations using elimination
* Use a system of nonlinear equations to solve applications

sections.title: Solve a System of Nonlinear Equations Using Graphing
sections.paragraph: We learned how to solve systems of linear equations with two variables by graphing, substitution and elimination. We will be using these same methods as we look at nonlinear systems of equations with two equations and two variables. A **system of nonlinear equations** is a system where at least one of the equations is not linear.

sections.title: Solve a System of Nonlinear Equations Using Substitution
sections.paragraph: The graphing method works well when the points of intersection are integers and so easy to read off the graph. But more often it is difficult to read the coordinates of the points of intersection. The substitution method is an algebraic method that will work well in many situations. It works especially well when it is easy to solve one of the equations for one of the variables.

sections.title: Solve a System of Nonlinear Equations Using Elimination
sections.paragraph: When we studied systems of linear equations, we used the method of elimination to solve the system. We can also use elimination to solve systems of nonlinear equations. It works well when the equations have both variables squared. When using elimination, we try to make the coefficients of one variable to be opposites, so when we add the equations together, that variable is eliminated.

sections.title: Use a System of Nonlinear Equations to Solve Applications
sections.paragraph: Systems of nonlinear equations can be used to model and solve many applications. We will look at an everyday geometric situation as our example.

chapters.title: Sequences
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Write the first few terms of a sequence
* Find a formula for the general term (nth term) of a sequence
* Use factorial notation
* Find the partial sum
* Use summation notation to write a sum

sections.title: Write the First Few Terms of a Sequence
sections.paragraph: Let’s look at the function $f\left(x\right)=2x$ and evaluate it for just the counting numbers.

sections.title: Find a Formula for the General Term (*n*th Term) of a Sequence
sections.paragraph: Sometimes we have a few terms of a sequence and it would be helpful to know the general term or *n*th term. To find the general term, we look for patterns in the terms. Often the patterns involve multiples or powers. We also look for a pattern in the signs of the terms.

sections.title: Use Factorial Notation
sections.paragraph: Sequences often have terms that are products of consecutive integers. We indicate these products with a special notation called *factorial notation*. For example,$5!$, read 5 factorial, means $5·4·3·2·1.$ The exclamation point is not punctuation here; it indicates the factorial notation.

sections.title: Find the Partial Sum
sections.paragraph: Sometimes in applications, rather than just list the terms, it is important for us to add the terms of a sequence. Rather than just connect the terms with plus signs, we can use summation notation.

sections.title: Use Summation Notation to Write a Sum
sections.paragraph: In the last two examples, we went from summation notation to writing out the sum. Now we will start with a sum and change it to summation notation. This is very similar to finding the general term of a sequence. We will need to look at the terms and find a pattern. Often the patterns involve multiples or powers.

chapters.title: Arithmetic Sequences
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Determine if a sequence is arithmetic
* Find the general term ($n$th term) of an arithmetic sequence
* Find the sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic sequence

sections.title: Determine if a Sequence is Arithmetic
sections.paragraph: The last section introduced sequences and now we will look at two specific types of sequences that each have special properties. In this section we will look at arithmetic sequences and in the next section, geometric sequences.

sections.title: Find the General Term (*n*th Term) of an Arithmetic Sequence
sections.paragraph: Just as we found a formula for the general term of a sequence, we can also find a formula for the general term of an arithmetic sequence.

sections.title: Find the Sum of the First *n* Terms of an Arithmetic Sequence
sections.paragraph: As with the general sequences, it is often useful to find the sum of an arithmetic sequence. The sum, ${S}_{n},$ of the first $n$ terms of any arithmetic sequence is written as ${S}_{n}={a}_{1}+{a}_{2}+{a}_{3}+...+{a}_{n}.$ To find the sum by merely adding all the terms can be tedious. So we can also develop a formula to find the sum of a sequence using the first and last term of the sequence.

chapters.title: Geometric Sequences and Series
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Determine if a sequence is geometric
* Find the general term (nth term) of a geometric sequence
* Find the sum of the first $n$ terms of a geometric sequence
* Find the sum of an infinite geometric series
* Apply geometric sequences and series in the real world

sections.title: Determine if a Sequence is Geometric
sections.paragraph: We are now ready to look at the second special type of sequence, the geometric sequence.

sections.title: Find the General Term (*n*th Term) of a Geometric Sequence
sections.paragraph: Just as we found a formula for the general term of a sequence and an arithmetic sequence, we can also find a formula for the general term of a geometric sequence.

sections.title: Find the Sum of the First *n* Terms of a Geometric Sequence
sections.paragraph: We found the sum of both general sequences and arithmetic sequence. We will now do the same for geometric sequences. The sum,${S}_{n},$ of the first *n* terms of a geometric sequence is written as ${S}_{n}={a}_{1}+{a}_{2}+{a}_{3}+...+{a}_{n}.$ We can write this sum by starting with the first term, ${a}_{1},$ and keep multiplying by *r* to get the next term as:

sections.title: Find the Sum of an Infinite Geometric Series
sections.paragraph: If we take a geometric sequence and add the terms, we have a sum that is called a geometric series. An infinite geometric series is an infinite sum whose first term is ${a}_{1}$ and common ratio is *r* and is written

sections.title: Apply Geometric Sequences and Series in the Real World
sections.paragraph: One application of geometric sequences has to do with consumer spending. If a tax rebate is given to each household, the effect on the economy is many times the amount of the individual rebate.

chapters.title: Binomial Theorem
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Use Pascal’s Triangle to expand a binomial
* Evaluate a binomial coefficient
* Use the Binomial Theorem to expand a binomial

sections.title: Use Pascal’s Triangle to Expand a Binomial
sections.paragraph: In our previous work, we have squared binomials either by using FOIL or by using the Binomial Squares Pattern. We can also say that we expanded ${\left(a+b\right)}^{2}.$

sections.title: Evaluate a Binomial Coefficient
sections.paragraph: While Pascal’s Triangle is one method to expand a binomial, we will also look at another method. Before we get to that, we need to introduce some more factorial notation. This notation is not only used to expand binomials, but also in the study and use of probability.

sections.title: Use the Binomial Theorem to Expand a Binomial
sections.paragraph: We are now ready to use the alternate method of expanding binomials. The Binomial Theorem uses the same pattern for the variables, but uses the binomial coefficient for the coefficient of each term.

sections.title: About OpenStax
sections.paragraph: OpenStax is a nonprofit based at Rice University, and it’s our mission to improve student access to education. Our first openly licensed college textbook was published in 2012, and our library has since scaled to over 35 books for college and AP® Courses used by hundreds of thousands of students. OpenStax Tutor, our low-cost personalized learning tool, is being piloted in college courses throughout the country. Through our partnerships with philanthropic foundations and our alliance with other educational resource organizations, OpenStax is breaking down the most common barriers to learning and empowering students and instructors to succeed.

sections.title: About *Prealgebra 2e*
sections.paragraph: *Prealgebra 2e* is designed to meet scope and sequence requirements for a one-semester prealgebra course. The text introduces the fundamental concepts of algebra while addressing the needs of students with diverse backgrounds and learning styles. Each topic builds upon previously developed material to demonstrate the cohesiveness and structure of mathematics.

sections.title: Coverage and Scope
sections.paragraph: *Prealgebra 2e* takes a student-support approach in its presentation of the content. The beginning, in particular, is presented as a sequence of small steps so that students gain confidence in their ability to succeed in the course. The order of topics was carefully planned to emphasize the logical progression throughout the course and to facilitate a thorough understanding of each concept. As new ideas are presented, they are explicitly related to previous topics.

sections.title: Changes to the Second Edition
sections.paragraph: The *Prealgebra 2e* revision focused on mathematical clarity and accuracy. Every Example, Try-It, Section Exercise, Review Exercise, and Practice Test item was reviewed by multiple faculty experts, and then verified by authors. This intensive effort resulted in hundreds of changes to the text, problem language, answers, instructor solutions, and graphics.

chapters.title: Introduction to Whole Numbers
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Identify counting numbers and whole numbers
* Model whole numbers
* Identify the place value of a digit
* Use place value to name whole numbers
* Use place value to write whole numbers
* Round whole numbers

sections.title: Identify Counting Numbers and Whole Numbers
sections.paragraph: Learning algebra is similar to learning a language. You start with a basic vocabulary and then add to it as you go along. You need to practice often until the vocabulary becomes easy to you. The more you use the vocabulary, the more familiar it becomes.

sections.title: Model Whole Numbers
sections.paragraph: Our number system is called a place value system because the value of a digit depends on its position, or place, in a number. The number $537$ has a different value than the number $735.$ Even though they use the same digits, their value is different because of the different placement of the $7$ and the $5.$

sections.title: Identify the Place Value of a Digit
sections.paragraph: By looking at money and $\text{base-10}$ blocks, we saw that each place in a number has a different value. A place value chart is a useful way to summarize this information. The place values are separated into groups of three, called periods. The periods are *ones, thousands, millions, billions, trillions*, and so on. In a written number, commas separate the periods.

sections.title: Use Place Value to Name Whole Numbers
sections.paragraph: When you write a check, you write out the number in words as well as in digits. To write a number in words, write the number in each period followed by the name of the period without the ‘s’ at the end. Start with the digit at the left, which has the largest place value. The commas separate the periods, so wherever there is a comma in the number, write a comma between the words. The ones period, which has the smallest place value, is not named.

sections.title: Use Place Value to Write Whole Numbers
sections.paragraph: We will now reverse the process and write a number given in words as digits.

sections.title: Round Whole Numbers
sections.paragraph: In $2013,$ the U.S. Census Bureau reported the population of the state of New York as $19,651,127$ people. It might be enough to say that the population is approximately $20$ million. The word *approximately* means that $20$ million is not the exact population, but is close to the exact value.

chapters.title: Add Whole Numbers
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Use addition notation
* Model addition of whole numbers
* Add whole numbers without models
* Translate word phrases to math notation
* Add whole numbers in applications

sections.title: Use Addition Notation
sections.paragraph: A college student has a part-time job. Last week he worked $3$ hours on Monday and $4$ hours on Friday. To find the total number of hours he worked last week, he added $3$ and $4.$

sections.title: Model Addition of Whole Numbers
sections.paragraph: Addition is really just counting. We will model addition with $\text{base-10}$ blocks. Remember, a block represents $1$ and a rod represents $10.$ Let’s start by modeling the addition expression we just considered, $3+4.$

sections.title: Add Whole Numbers Without Models
sections.paragraph: Now that we have used models to add numbers, we can move on to adding without models. Before we do that, make sure you know all the one digit addition facts. You will need to use these number facts when you add larger numbers.

sections.title: Translate Word Phrases to Math Notation
sections.paragraph: Earlier in this section, we translated math notation into words. Now we’ll reverse the process. We’ll translate word phrases into math notation. Some of the word phrases that indicate addition are listed in [link].

sections.title: Add Whole Numbers in Applications
sections.paragraph: Now that we have practiced adding whole numbers, let’s use what we’ve learned to solve real-world problems. We’ll start by outlining a plan. First, we need to read the problem to determine what we are looking for. Then we write a word phrase that gives the information to find it. Next we translate the word phrase into math notation and then simplify. Finally, we write a sentence to answer the question.

chapters.title: Subtract Whole Numbers
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Use subtraction notation
* Model subtraction of whole numbers
* Subtract whole numbers
* Translate word phrases to math notation
* Subtract whole numbers in applications

sections.title: Use Subtraction Notation
sections.paragraph: Suppose there are seven bananas in a bowl. Elana uses three of them to make a smoothie. How many bananas are left in the bowl? To answer the question, we subtract three from seven. When we subtract, we take one number away from another to find the difference. The notation we use to subtract $3$ from $7$ is

sections.title: Model Subtraction of Whole Numbers
sections.paragraph: A model can help us visualize the process of subtraction much as it did with addition. Again, we will use $\text{base-10}$ blocks. Remember a block represents 1 and a rod represents 10. Let’s start by modeling the subtraction expression we just considered, $7-3.$

sections.title: Subtract Whole Numbers
sections.paragraph: Addition and subtraction are inverse operations. Addition undoes subtraction, and subtraction undoes addition.

sections.title: Translate Word Phrases to Math Notation
sections.paragraph: As with addition, word phrases can tell us to operate on two numbers using subtraction. To translate from a word phrase to math notation, we look for key words that indicate subtraction. Some of the words that indicate subtraction are listed in [link].

sections.title: Subtract Whole Numbers in Applications
sections.paragraph: To solve applications with subtraction, we will use the same plan that we used with addition. First, we need to determine what we are asked to find. Then we write a phrase that gives the information to find it. We translate the phrase into math notation and then simplify to get the answer. Finally, we write a sentence to answer the question, using the appropriate units.

chapters.title: Multiply Whole Numbers
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Use multiplication notation
* Model multiplication of whole numbers
* Multiply whole numbers
* Translate word phrases to math notation
* Multiply whole numbers in applications

sections.title: Use Multiplication Notation
sections.paragraph: Suppose you were asked to count all these pennies shown in [link].

sections.title: Model Multiplication of Whole Numbers
sections.paragraph: There are many ways to model multiplication. Unlike in the previous sections where we used $\text{base-10}$ blocks, here we will use counters to help us understand the meaning of multiplication. A counter is any object that can be used for counting. We will use round blue counters.

sections.title: Multiply Whole Numbers
sections.paragraph: In order to multiply without using models, you need to know all the one digit multiplication facts. Make sure you know them fluently before proceeding in this section.

sections.title: Translate Word Phrases to Math Notation
sections.paragraph: Earlier in this section, we translated math notation into words. Now we’ll reverse the process and translate word phrases into math notation. Some of the words that indicate multiplication are given in [link].

sections.title: Multiply Whole Numbers in Applications
sections.paragraph: We will use the same strategy we used previously to solve applications of multiplication. First, we need to determine what we are looking for. Then we write a phrase that gives the information to find it. We then translate the phrase into math notation and simplify to get the answer. Finally, we write a sentence to answer the question.

chapters.title: Divide Whole Numbers
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Use division notation
* Model division of whole numbers
* Divide whole numbers
* Translate word phrases to math notation
* Divide whole numbers in applications

sections.title: Use Division Notation
sections.paragraph: So far we have explored addition, subtraction, and multiplication. Now let’s consider division. Suppose you have the $12$ cookies in [link] and want to package them in bags with $4$ cookies in each bag. How many bags would we need?

sections.title: Model Division of Whole Numbers
sections.paragraph: As we did with multiplication, we will model division using counters. The operation of division helps us organize items into equal groups as we start with the number of items in the dividend and subtract the number in the divisor repeatedly.

sections.title: Divide Whole Numbers
sections.paragraph: We said that addition and subtraction are inverse operations because one undoes the other. Similarly, division is the inverse operation of multiplication. We know $12÷4=3$ because $3·4=12.$ Knowing all the multiplication number facts is very important when doing division.

sections.title: Translate Word Phrases to Math Notation
sections.paragraph: Earlier in this section, we translated math notation for division into words. Now we’ll translate word phrases into math notation. Some of the words that indicate division are given in [link].

sections.title: Divide Whole Numbers in Applications
sections.paragraph: We will use the same strategy we used in previous sections to solve applications. First, we determine what we are looking for. Then we write a phrase that gives the information to find it. We then translate the phrase into math notation and simplify it to get the answer. Finally, we write a sentence to answer the question.

chapters.title: Introduction to the Language of Algebra
Use the Language of Algebra
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Use variables and algebraic symbols
* Identify expressions and equations
* Simplify expressions with exponents
* Simplify expressions using the order of operations

sections.title: Use Variables and Algebraic Symbols
sections.paragraph: Greg and Alex have the same birthday, but they were born in different years. This year Greg is $20$ years old and Alex is $23,$ so Alex is $3$ years older than Greg. When Greg was $12,$ Alex was $15.$ When Greg is $35,$ Alex will be $38.$ No matter what Greg’s age is, Alex’s age will always be $3$ years more, right?

sections.title: Identify Expressions and Equations
sections.paragraph: What is the difference in English between a phrase and a sentence? A phrase expresses a single thought that is incomplete by itself, but a sentence makes a complete statement. “Running very fast” is a phrase, but “The football player was running very fast” is a sentence. A sentence has a subject and a verb.

sections.title: Simplify Expressions with Exponents
sections.paragraph: To simplify a numerical expression means to do all the math possible. For example, to simplify $4·2+1$ we’d first multiply $4·2$ to get $8$ and then add the $1$ to get $9.$ A good habit to develop is to work down the page, writing each step of the process below the previous step. The example just described would look like this:

sections.title: Simplify Expressions Using the Order of Operations
sections.paragraph: We’ve introduced most of the symbols and notation used in algebra, but now we need to clarify the order of operations. Otherwise, expressions may have different meanings, and they may result in different values.

chapters.title: Evaluate, Simplify, and Translate Expressions
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Evaluate algebraic expressions
* Identify terms, coefficients, and like terms
* Simplify expressions by combining like terms
* Translate word phrases to algebraic expressions

sections.title: Evaluate Algebraic Expressions
sections.paragraph: In the last section, we simplified expressions using the order of operations. In this section, we’ll evaluate expressions—again following the order of operations.

sections.title: Identify Terms, Coefficients, and Like Terms
sections.paragraph: Algebraic expressions are made up of *terms*. A term is a constant or the product of a constant and one or more variables. Some examples of terms are $7,y,5{x}^{2},9a,\text{and}{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}13xy.$

sections.title: Simplify Expressions by Combining Like Terms
sections.paragraph: We can simplify an expression by combining the like terms. What do you think $3x+6x$ would simplify to? If you thought $9x,$ you would be right!

sections.title: Translate Words to Algebraic Expressions
sections.paragraph: In the previous section, we listed many operation symbols that are used in algebra, and then we translated expressions and equations into word phrases and sentences. Now we’ll reverse the process and translate word phrases into algebraic expressions. The symbols and variables we’ve talked about will help us do that. They are summarized in [link].

chapters.title: Solving Equations Using the Subtraction and Addition Properties of Equality
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Determine whether a number is a solution of an equation
* Model the Subtraction Property of Equality
* Solve equations using the Subtraction Property of Equality
* Solve equations using the Addition Property of Equality
* Translate word phrases to algebraic equations
* Translate to an equation and solve

sections.title: Determine Whether a Number is a Solution of an Equation
sections.paragraph: Solving an equation is like discovering the answer to a puzzle. An algebraic equation states that two algebraic expressions are equal. To solve an equation is to determine the values of the variable that make the equation a true statement. Any number that makes the equation true is called a solution of the equation. It is the answer to the puzzle!

sections.title: Model the Subtraction Property of Equality
sections.paragraph: We will use a model to help you understand how the process of solving an equation is like solving a puzzle. An envelope represents the variable – since its contents are unknown – and each counter represents one.

sections.title: Solve Equations Using the Subtraction Property of Equality
sections.paragraph: Our puzzle has given us an idea of what we need to do to solve an equation. The goal is to isolate the variable by itself on one side of the equations. In the previous examples, we used the Subtraction Property of Equality, which states that when we subtract the same quantity from both sides of an equation, we still have equality.

sections.title: Solve Equations Using the Addition Property of Equality
sections.paragraph: In all the equations we have solved so far, a number was added to the variable on one side of the equation. We used subtraction to “undo” the addition in order to isolate the variable.

sections.title: Translate Word Phrases to Algebraic Equations
sections.paragraph: Remember, an equation has an equal sign between two algebraic expressions. So if we have a sentence that tells us that two phrases are equal, we can translate it into an equation. We look for clue words that mean *equals*. Some words that translate to the equal sign are:

sections.title: Translate to an Equation and Solve
sections.paragraph: Now let’s practice translating sentences into algebraic equations and then solving them. We will solve the equations by using the Subtraction and Addition Properties of Equality.

chapters.title: Find Multiples and Factors
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Identify multiples of numbers
* Use common divisibility tests
* Find all the factors of a number
* Identify prime and composite numbers

sections.title: Identify Multiples of Numbers
sections.paragraph: Annie is counting the shoes in her closet. The shoes are matched in pairs, so she doesn’t have to count each one. She counts by twos: $2,4,6,8,10,12.$ She has $12$ shoes in her closet.

sections.title: Use Common Divisibility Tests
sections.paragraph: Another way to say that $375$ is a multiple of $5$ is to say that $375$ is divisible by $5.$ In fact, $375÷5$ is $75,$ so $375$ is $5\cdot 75.$ Notice in [link] that $10,519$ is not a multiple $3.$ When we divided $10,519$ by $3$ we did not get a counting number, so $10,519$ is not divisible by $3.$

sections.title: Find All the Factors of a Number
sections.paragraph:
There are often several ways to talk about the same idea. So
far, we’ve seen that if $m$ is a multiple of $n,$ we can say that $m$ is divisible by $n.$ We know that $72$ is the product of $8$ and $9,$ so we can say $72$ is a multiple of $8$ and $72$ is a multiple of $9.$ We can also say $72$ is divisible by $8$ and by $9.$ Another way to talk about this is to say that $8$ and $9$ are factors of $72.$ When we write $72=8\cdot 9$ we can say that we have factored $72.$

sections.title: Identify Prime and Composite Numbers
sections.paragraph: Some numbers, like $72,$ have many factors. Other numbers, such as $7,$ have only two factors: $1$ and the number. A number with only two factors is called a prime number. A number with more than two factors is called a composite number. The number $1$ is neither prime nor composite. It has only one factor, itself.

chapters.title: Prime Factorization and the Least Common Multiple
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Find the prime factorization of a composite number
* Find the least common multiple (LCM) of two numbers

sections.title: Find the Prime Factorization of a Composite Number
sections.paragraph: In the previous section, we found the factors of a number. Prime numbers have only two factors, the number $1$ and the prime number itself. Composite numbers have more than two factors, and every composite number can be written as a unique product of primes. This is called the prime factorization of a number. When we write the prime factorization of a number, we are rewriting the number as a product of primes. Finding the prime factorization of a composite number will help you later in this course.

sections.title: Find the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of Two Numbers
sections.paragraph: One of the reasons we look at multiples and primes is to use these techniques to find the least common multiple of two numbers. This will be useful when we add and subtract fractions with different denominators.

chapters.title: Introduction to Integers
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Locate positive and negative numbers on the number line
* Order positive and negative numbers
* Find opposites
* Simplify expressions with absolute value
* Translate word phrases to expressions with integers

sections.title: Locate Positive and Negative Numbers on the Number Line
sections.paragraph: Do you live in a place that has very cold winters? Have you ever experienced a temperature below zero? If so, you are already familiar with negative numbers. A negative number is a number that is less than $0.$ Very cold temperatures are measured in degrees below zero and can be described by negative numbers. For example, $-1\text{°F}$ (read as “negative one degree Fahrenheit”) is $1{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}\text{degree}$ below $0.$ A minus sign is shown before a number to indicate that it is negative. [link] shows $-20\text{°F},$ which is $20{\rule{0.2em}{0ex}}\text{degrees}$ below $0.$

sections.title: Order Positive and Negative Numbers
sections.paragraph: We can use the number line to compare and order positive and negative numbers. Going from left to right, numbers increase in value. Going from right to left, numbers decrease in value. See [link].

sections.title: Find Opposites
sections.paragraph: On the number line, the negative numbers are a mirror image of the positive numbers with zero in the middle. Because the numbers $2$ and $-2$ are the same distance from zero, they are called opposites. The opposite of $2$ is $-2,$ and the opposite of $-2$ is $2$ as shown in [link](a). Similarly, $3$ and $-3$ are opposites as shown in [link](b).

sections.title: Simplify Expressions with Absolute Value
sections.paragraph: We saw that numbers such as $5$ and $-5$ are opposites because they are the same distance from $0$ on the number line. They are both five units from $0.$ The distance between $0$ and any number on the number line is called the absolute value of that number. Because distance is never negative, the absolute value of any number is never negative.

sections.title: Translate Word Phrases into Expressions with Integers
sections.paragraph: Now we can translate word phrases into expressions with integers. Look for words that indicate a negative sign. For example, the word *negative* in “negative twenty” indicates $-20.$ So does the word *opposite* in “the opposite of $20\text{.”}$

chapters.title: Add Integers
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Model addition of integers
* Simplify expressions with integers
* Evaluate variable expressions with integers
* Translate word phrases to algebraic expressions
* Add integers in applications

sections.title: Model Addition of Integers
sections.paragraph: Now that we have located positive and negative numbers on the number line, it is time to discuss arithmetic operations with integers.

sections.title: Simplify Expressions with Integers
sections.paragraph: Now that you have modeled adding small positive and negative integers, you can visualize the model in your mind to simplify expressions with any integers.

sections.title: Evaluate Variable Expressions with Integers
sections.paragraph: Remember that to evaluate an expression means to substitute a number for the variable in the expression. Now we can use negative numbers as well as positive numbers when evaluating expressions.

sections.title: Translate Word Phrases to Algebraic Expressions
sections.paragraph: All our earlier work translating word phrases to algebra also applies to expressions that include both positive and negative numbers. Remember that the phrase *the sum* indicates addition.

sections.title: Add Integers in Applications
sections.paragraph: Recall that we were introduced to some situations in everyday life that use positive and negative numbers, such as temperatures, banking, and sports. For example, a debt of $\text{5}$ could be represented as $\text{−5.}$ Let’s practice translating and solving a few applications.

chapters.title: Subtract Integers
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Model subtraction of integers
* Simplify expressions with integers
* Evaluate variable expressions with integers
* Translate words phrases to algebraic expressions
* Subtract integers in applications

sections.title: Model Subtraction of Integers
sections.paragraph: Remember the story in the last section about the toddler and the cookies? Children learn how to subtract numbers through their everyday experiences. Real-life experiences serve as models for subtracting positive numbers, and in some cases, such as temperature, for adding negative as well as positive numbers. But it is difficult to relate subtracting negative numbers to common life experiences. Most people do not have an intuitive understanding of subtraction when negative numbers are involved. Math teachers use several different models to explain subtracting negative numbers.

sections.title: Simplify Expressions with Integers
sections.paragraph: Do you see a pattern? Are you ready to subtract integers without counters? Let’s do two more subtractions. We’ll think about how we would model these with counters, but we won’t actually use the counters.

sections.title: Evaluate Variable Expressions with Integers
sections.paragraph: Now we’ll practice evaluating expressions that involve subtracting negative numbers as well as positive numbers.

sections.title: Translate Word Phrases to Algebraic Expressions
sections.paragraph: When we first introduced the operation symbols, we saw that the expression $a-b$ may be read in several ways as shown below.

sections.title: Subtract Integers in Applications
sections.paragraph: It’s hard to find something if we don’t know what we’re looking for or what to call it. So when we solve an application problem, we first need to determine what we are asked to find. Then we can write a phrase that gives the information to find it. We’ll translate the phrase into an expression and then simplify the expression to get the answer. Finally, we summarize the answer in a sentence to make sure it makes sense.

chapters.title: Multiply and Divide Integers
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Multiply integers
* Divide integers
* Simplify expressions with integers
* Evaluate variable expressions with integers
* Translate word phrases to algebraic expressions

sections.title: Multiply Integers
sections.paragraph: Since multiplication is mathematical shorthand for repeated addition, our counter model can easily be applied to show multiplication of integers. Let’s look at this concrete model to see what patterns we notice. We will use the same examples that we used for addition and subtraction.

sections.title: Divide Integers
sections.paragraph: Division is the inverse operation of multiplication. So, $15÷3=5$ because $5·3=15$ In words, this expression says that $\mathbf{\text{15}}$ can be divided into $\mathbf{\text{3}}$ groups of $\mathbf{\text{5}}$ each because adding five three times gives $\mathbf{\text{15}}.$ If we look at some examples of multiplying integers, we might figure out the rules for dividing integers.

sections.title: Simplify Expressions with Integers
sections.paragraph: Now we’ll simplify expressions that use all four operations–addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division–with integers. Remember to follow the order of operations.

sections.title: Evaluate Variable Expressions with Integers
sections.paragraph: Now we can evaluate expressions that include multiplication and division with integers. Remember that to evaluate an expression, substitute the numbers in place of the variables, and then simplify.

sections.title: Translate Word Phrases to Algebraic Expressions
sections.paragraph: Once again, all our prior work translating words to algebra transfers to phrases that include both multiplying and dividing integers. Remember that the key word for multiplication is *product* and for division is *quotient*.

chapters.title: Solve Equations Using Integers; The Division Property of Equality
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Determine whether an integer is a solution of an equation
* Solve equations with integers using the Addition and Subtraction Properties of Equality
* Model the Division Property of Equality
* Solve equations using the Division Property of Equality
* Translate to an equation and solve

sections.title: Determine Whether a Number is a Solution of an Equation
sections.paragraph: In Solve Equations with the Subtraction and Addition Properties of Equality, we saw that a solution of an equation is a value of a variable that makes a true statement when substituted into that equation. In that section, we found solutions that were whole numbers. Now that we’ve worked with integers, we’ll find integer solutions to equations.

sections.title: Solve Equations with Integers Using the Addition and Subtraction Properties of Equality
sections.paragraph: In Solve Equations with the Subtraction and Addition Properties of Equality, we solved equations similar to the two shown here using the Subtraction and Addition Properties of Equality. Now we can use them again with integers.

sections.title: Model the Division Property of Equality
sections.paragraph: All of the equations we have solved so far have been of the form $x+a=b$ or $x-a=b.$ We were able to isolate the variable by adding or subtracting the constant term. Now we’ll see how to solve equations that involve division.

sections.title: Solve Equations Using the Division Property of Equality
sections.paragraph: The previous examples lead to the Division Property of Equality. When you divide both sides of an equation by any nonzero number, you still have equality.

sections.title: Translate to an Equation and Solve
sections.paragraph: In the past several examples, we were given an equation containing a variable. In the next few examples, we’ll have to first translate word sentences into equations with variables and then we will solve the equations.

chapters.title: Visualize Fractions
chapters.abstract:
By the end of this section, you will be able to:

* Understand the meaning of fractions
* Model improper fractions and mixed numbers
* Convert between improper fractions and mixed numbers
* Model equivalent fractions
* Find equivalent fractions
* Locate fractions and mixed numbers on the number line
* Order fractions and mixed numbers

sections.title: Understand the Meaning of Fractions
sections.paragraph: Andy and Bobby love pizza. On Monday night, they share a pizza equally. How much of the pizza does each one get? Are you thinking that each boy gets half of the pizza?
